“In this respect it is potentially a gamechanger,” says de Silva, who co-led the study with his colleague Dr Kevin Cheng. It was based on observation of 491 people with refractory angina between 2014 and 2024, 474 of whom had the implant fitted at 19 hospitals in England and Scotland.
Most patients went home the day of the procedure or the day after and serious complications were rare, the study also found.
According to de Silva, it shows that the device can greatly reduce the debilitating symptoms of refractory angina that significantly compromise quality of life and the ability to undertake normal day to day activities, and can help people avoid being admitted to hospital and boost their mental wellbeing.
“Many patients report their lives being transformed and that it helps them to achieve the quality of life they wish for, that they were unable to enjoy prior to the reducer implant – they get their life back,” says de Silva.
Despite the apparent success of the implant, and that only “a tiny fraction” of the 300,000 people with refractory angina have had one fitted, it is too early to yet see CSR as a standard treatment for people with this very painful form of coronary artery disease, he says.
More trials are needed and the NHS needs to approve the funding needed to expand access, he adds.
Dr Sonya Babu-Narayan, a consultant cardiologist and the British Heart Foundation’s clinical director, said: “The findings are reassuring as they show that in routine clinical practice the device is being delivered safely and is resulting in fewer symptoms for patients.”
The device “offers hope for people living with this challenging condition”, she said.
summary: A new experimental chest implant called a coronary sinus reducer offers significant relief for patients suffering from refractory angina, a debilitating form of heart disease. A recent study of 491 patients found that the hourglass-shaped device successfully reduced chest pain in 75% of individuals within six months of implantation. While the procedure has proven safe and transformative for patients like Cristian Jensen, further trials and NHS funding approvals are required before it becomes a standard treatment.
key_points: Refractory angina affects an estimated 300,000 people in England whose symptoms persist despite medication, stents, and bypass surgery.
The coronary sinus reducer is a small, hourglass-shaped device inserted via keyhole surgery in the neck that redirects blood flow to oxygen-deprived heart muscle.
A major study found that the implant significantly reduced chest pain in 75% of patients within six months.
Despite promising results and safe outcomes, the implant remains an experimental treatment that requires more trials and NHS funding to become standard practice.

title: 'I had 9 organs removed after true cause of pain discovered' - AOL
author: Steven Smith
content:
![Mirror UK](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/logos/light/mirror-uk.png?v=1784567839)
![Claire Gerring in hospital](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/08/23/cbaec5b1-c16d-3387-b0ba-e5b6d1f4af3d/d2236bf9-23c9-4961-8401-0a38df3cbc69.jpg)
A woman's condition turned out to be so rare that it required nine of her organs to be removed during “the mother of all surgeries”.
Claire Gerring, 42, had initially been referred to John Radcliffe Hospital after an ultrasound in November 2022 with suspected endometriosis and was put on the wait list in May 2023 for an investigative laparoscopy. But after intense pain on her right side, a positive Faecal Immunochemical Test (FIT) test led to a colonoscopy.
Doctors discovered her appendix was inverted and a CT scan revealed she had malignant tissue on the organ and needed investigative surgery. A biopsy on May 6, 2025, confirmed she had stage four Pseudomyxoma Peritonei (PMP) - a rare cancer that typically originates from a tumour in the appendix.
She was referred to Basingstoke and North Hampshire Hospital, as it is one of only two hospitals that specialise in PMP. The cancer in her appendix had ruptured, meaning there were other nodules in the rest of her body.
![Claire Gerring after her first hospital discharge](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/08/23/cbaec5b1-c16d-3387-b0ba-e5b6d1f4af3d/58be2c1e-5f69-4883-a3f0-8be146c17046.jpg)
On July 15, 2025, Claire, who is mum to sons Oscar, 15, and Spencer, 14, underwent a 10-hour operation to remove nine organs - her appendix, ovaries, fallopian tubes, gall bladder, spleen, uterus and cervix.
She also had removed her greater omentum, belly button, peritoneum lining and part of her bowel Her liver was also partially cut away, as well as having her diaphragm scraped and bladder stripped.
During the surgery Claire had HIPEC chemotherapy – heated chemotherapy circulated around her abdomen. After four-and-a-half weeks in hospital, she was discharged and has been left with bowel problems, but has no evidence of disease at the moment and will be monitored for the next 20 years.
Claire, a hairdresser from Wantage, Oxfordshire, said: “I felt really quite scared and quite alone after my diagnosis. When you’ve got a rare cancer and it’s not something you’ve heard of before, there are not a lot of people to talk to about it.
“I was told by surgeons before my operation what they would remove. On top of that they cut part of my liver away and scraped my diaphragm and stripped my bladder.
“It’s a lot to process. It’s quite scary, but I’m lucky I had professionals who knew what they were doing. It’s called the mother of all surgeries because of the severity of it."
After struggling with pain in her side and asking for her laparoscopy surgery to be expedited by her GP, a positive FIT test and colonoscopy in March 2025 revealed Claire’s inverted appendix, which needed a CT scan. Her original endometriosis surgery was set to go ahead on April 11, 2025.
“But on April 10, I phoned up just to double check they’d got my CT scan results back as the next day I was now having investigative surgery,” Claire told Talk to the Press. “That’s where I was told I had malignant tissues in my appendix.
“At that point I wasn’t too worried because I thought, ‘well I don’t need my appendix’. Thirty seconds later, my gynaecology lady rang and said ‘Claire this is serious’ and that my surgery wouldn’t be happening tomorrow."
![Claire Gerring with her husband, Tom](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/08/23/cbaec5b1-c16d-3387-b0ba-e5b6d1f4af3d/db0e4351-e120-4d01-a6ad-72df6949af9a.jpg)
Investigative surgery on May 6 revealed the cancer was not contained to her appendix.
“When the tumour ruptures it releases mucin, which is a jelly-like substance,” Claire said. “It’s often called ‘jelly belly’. Your abdomen fills up and coats all your organs with mucin."
As a result, Claire needed vital cytoreductive surgery with HIPEC to remove all her affected organs.
"I’m coming up to my year's anniversary and I’m still left with complications in my bowel and I’ve been back in hospital in between,” she said. “With a lot of cancer you’re told you lose weight, but with this one I put on weight and looked four months pregnant.
“I thought I’d just got to 40 and it was my middle-aged spread. But it was actually inside my abdomen.
“Recovery is a slow process, obviously, like most surgeries, if you have your appendix out the recovery time is six to eight weeks.
“Times that by 11 (and) it’s a long time. I had a bowel obstruction and was back in hospital for a 10-day stay recently.
“I’m still grateful, it’s a small price to pay. Basically what they say is you’re never back to your old self, you just get used to the new you."
Now a year into her recovery, Claire has thrown herself into fundraising for charity Pseudomyxoma Survivor, throwing a masked ball on July 11, 2026.
On the night, she said: "I just feel my main purpose for doing this is raising awareness about the rare cancer and Pseudomyxoma Survivor. I believe deeply that if you’re willing to take, you must also be willing to give back. And here I am today, standing in front of you, living that promise.
"I feel so passionate about giving back to this charity which stepped in and helped me at the point in life when it felt uncertain and alone. They also support research and have recently given £100,000 towards — would you believe it — the research project is called The Beacon Project.
"They are creating a blood test to detect the cancer and recurrence way before CTs can even pick it up. Tonight, we are part of supporting these amazing breakthroughs."
![Tom, Spencer, Claire and Oscar](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/08/23/cbaec5b1-c16d-3387-b0ba-e5b6d1f4af3d/0e9204ee-40fc-490f-8b92-a9e6fe9d0c45.jpg)
She has raised £16,002 so far for the charity through Just Giving and other events.
Maddy Lomas, trustee at Pseudomyxoma Survivor, said: “As a charity, we are incredibly touched by the effort and generosity behind this fundraising event. What makes it even more special is that it has been organised by someone who knows first-hand what it means to face a diagnosis of PMP.
"Having received support from Pseudomyxoma Survivor during her own journey, Claire has now turned that experience into an opportunity to give back and support others who are walking a similar path. This is truly commendable and a wonderful example of how personal experiences can be transformed into something that brings hope and support to others.
"For a small charity, the £16,002 raised is incredibly significant and will have a lasting impact. It will help us continue our mission of providing support to people affected by PMP, raising awareness of this rare disease, and contributing towards vital research that can make a difference for the future.
"However, just as important is the much-needed awareness Claire has created by organising and delivering this event. For a rare disease like PMP, every person who learns about the condition helps to increase understanding and could make a life-changing difference by helping someone recognise the signs, seek support, or feel less alone following their own diagnosis.”
summary: Claire Gerring, a 42-year-old hairdresser, underwent a grueling 10-hour surgery to remove nine organs after being diagnosed with stage four Pseudomyxoma Peritonei (PMP), a rare cancer that typically originates from the appendix. Following a colonoscopy and biopsy in May 2025, doctors discovered her appendix had ruptured, spreading the disease throughout her abdomen. Today, she has no evidence of disease and is raising awareness and funds for the charity Pseudomyxoma Survivor.
key_points: Claire Gerring was initially suspected of having endometriosis before a colonoscopy and CT scan revealed malignant tissue on her inverted appendix.
She was diagnosed with stage four Pseudomyxoma Peritonei (PMP), a rare cancer that causes a jelly-like substance called mucin to coat the abdominal organs.

In July 2025, she underwent major surgery to remove nine organs—including her appendix, ovaries, fallopian tubes, gall bladder, spleen, uterus, and cervix—alongside receiving heated chemotherapy (HIPEC).
She currently shows no evidence of disease, is monitored regularly, and has raised over £16,000 for the charity Pseudomyxoma Survivor to support awareness and research.

title: Reading's Rutherford Cancer Centre to reopen after four years
author: Drew Hyndman
content:
![Mark Middleton, a middle aged white man with short grey hair, smiles at the camera. He is wearing a blue suit jacket and a white shirt with the top button undone. He is stood in front of Reading town centre.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/0ea6/live/51035e30-9d91-11f1-b553-7db031e5e7ab.jpg)
Mark Middleton says Icon Group chose the building because of the "world class" facilities inside
- Published
A cancer centre which closed after the company running it went out of business is set to reopen under new owners.
The Rutherford Centre initially opened for cancer patients to great fanfare in 2018, offering the latest cutting edge treatments.
In 2022 the company running it closed, blaming the Covid-19 pandemic, and the building has lay empty ever since.
Icon Group, an Australian healthcare company with several existing UK clinics, plans to open in the same building as soon as 2027.
The previous owners had taken on NHS contracts, as well as private patients, and Mark Middleton, Group CEO of Icon Group, says that's something they're keen to explore: "We believe in access for everyone, and we also believe in the great strength of public-private partnerships."
He adds : "I see really no reason why those partnerships can't be part of the solution for the wait times for cancer care in the UK."
Doctors have warned in the past that patients are waiting too long for diagnosis and treatment.
![Steve Allen, a white man in his 70s with grey hair and unframed glasses smiles at the camera. He's in a button up pink shirt with the top button undone. He is sat in a park with browned grass and a tree behind him.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/7b69/live/ed489280-9d8a-11f1-adf5-2dc21c9cc109.jpg)
Steve Allen was treated for prostate cancer at Royal Berkshire Hospital
Steve Allen, a former consultant aneasthetist at Royal Berkshire Hospital, was treated for prostate cancer at the hospital.
He says private companies providing treatment for the NHS is something people "either love or hate".
"There is no doubt in my mind that without private medicine in the NHS you wouldn't be able to cope with the demand," he says.
One of the big barriers to meeting that demand, Allen says, is shortage of staff.
"It takes five years at least to get somebody to a level where they might sometimes be able to work independently."
![The Rutherford centre, a two story red brick building with a section of glass frontage on one half of the ground floor.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/f430/live/11676f90-9d97-11f1-9233-8716b68cda7b.jpg)
The Rutherford Centre went out of business in 2022 and has laid empty ever since.
It's a challenge they're prepared for and Middleton says "we have quite a lot of Australians coming over".
"We're also going to hire local people as well, absolutely. I think there's a great mix."
The BBC has approached Royal Berkshire Hospital Trust for comment.
summary: The Rutherford Cancer Centre in Reading, which closed in 2022 after its previous operator went out of business, is scheduled to reopen under new ownership by Australian healthcare company Icon Group as early as 2027. The facility originally opened in 2018 and has remained empty since its closure, which was blamed on the Covid-19 pandemic. New leadership plans to explore public-private partnerships with the NHS and intends to hire both local staff and international workers to address staffing challenges.
key_points: The Rutherford Centre in Reading will reopen under new owners after closing in 2022.
Australian healthcare company Icon Group plans to reopen the facility by 2027.
The new owners are keen to explore public-private partnerships to help address UK cancer care wait times.
Icon Group plans to hire a mix of local staff and personnel from Australia to overcome staffing shortages.

title: Rectal cancer trial offers non-surgical treatment hope
author: Tim Dale
content:
![A group of doctors wearing green scrubs preparing to operate on a patient](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/22d4/live/991dab00-9baa-11f1-92e6-b1dfcecd4308.jpg)
Those behind the survey believe it will mean that for some patients life-changing major surgery may be avoided
- Published
A major trial has found that patients with rectal cancer may be able to avoid major surgery and the need for a colostomy bag.
Led by the Universities of Leeds and Birmingham, the international trial treated patients with early-stage rectal cancer, with combinations of chemotherapy and radiotherapy instead of surgery.
The findings, published in Lancet Oncology and funded by Cancer Research UK, said the initial results suggested that organâpreserving treatment may be a realistic option for many people with early rectal cancer.
Cancer Research UK said the findings could be "life-changing for thousands of people".
Up to 14,000 people are diagnosed with rectal cancer in the UK every year and of these, around one in three are at an early stage, according to the University of Leeds.
Patients are usually treated with a complex surgical procedure called a Total Mesorectal Excision (TME), which involves the complete removal of the rectum, the surrounding fat, and lymph nodes.
It has a high cure rate, but can have a significant impact and may also require a temporary or permanent colostomy bag.
The trial, named STAR-TREC, set out to discover whether organ-preserving treatments - radiotherapy and chemotherapy - could help patients avoid surgery while keeping the cancer under control.
![A smiling man and woman stood side by side. The woman has long blonde hair and is wearing a blue open shirt with a black t-shirt underneath. The man is wearing glasses and a blue t-shirt. They are standing in an outdoor setting with a green bush behind them.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/891/cpsprodpb/da4f/live/eed88760-9ef5-11f1-aed4-af6fe65bfcd6.png)
Hugh Chown has been supported through his treatment by his daughter Rachel
Hugh Chown, 65, from Harrogate, was diagnosed with rectal cancer at Leeds Cancer Centre after contacting his GP after a few months of occasional bleeding.
"I got the diagnosis â it was totally unexpected. I was shocked but accepting of it. I knew worrying wouldn't help, so I just focused on living life."
He said his consultant told him about the clinical trial two weeks later.
"She explained that the usual treatment would be surgery and it was highly likely I'd be left with a permanent colostomy bag."
He said she told him she thought he had a good chance of a positive outcome from the trial and said the decision to participate "wasn't difficult".
Hugh said the "worst-case scenario" was that it would not work and he would still need surgery.
His treatment consisted of taking tablets twice a day and receiving one radiotherapy session a day, five days a week for five weeks.
"For the first two weeks, the side effects were minimal but by the middle of the third week, I started to feel run down and tired and this got worse as the treatment went on.
"The fatigue also continued to get worse for a few weeks after the treatment stopped."
He said the effects took about six months to wear off completely, but it had a minimal impact compared to major surgery and a permanent colostomy bag.
"The consultant said I'd had a perfect result and the cancer was gone, but because it was part of the trial, I had another [colonoscopy] at 16 weeks and all was still clear."
He said after that he moved on to regular checks for the trial and then the standard NHS cancer checks for a further two weeks.
"My last check was in May this year and everything was fine," he addd.
Hugh's first wife died from bowel cancer at the age of 41 and he was supported through his treatment by his daughter, Rachel.
The 33-year-old is associate director of research and innovation at the Christie NHS Foundation Trust in Manchester, a specialist cancer treatment centre.
"I was nine when my mum died of bowel cancer, but outcomes now are very different," she said.
"I felt fortunate because my work in cancer care and research helped me understand the choices Dad was offered, and what they meant. When I heard about the trial, I felt strongly that it was his best option."
![A man pictured in a clinical setting. He has balding hair, is wearing glasses and a light blue shirt with a pink tie.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/932/cpsprodpb/6c5f/live/44d490b0-9efa-11f1-aed4-af6fe65bfcd6.png)
Prof David Sebag-Montefiore said the results were an example of how "kinder radiotherapy treatment" may avoid the need for major surgery
More than 400 patients were recruited at cancer centres across Europe for the trial, which was co-led by Prof David Sebag-Montefiore in Leeds and Prof Simon Bach at UCL, and was co-ordinated by the University of Birmingham,
Prof Sebag-Montefiore said the "exciting results" were an example of how a "smarter, kinder radiotherapy treatment may allow patients to avoid the need for major surgery".
He said: "It is gratifying that patients experienced a relatively low level of severe short-term side effects as a result of the smaller, more targeted radiotherapy approach that we specifically developed for STAR-TREC."
Prof Bach at UCL said "for decades" patients had been asked to accept the loss of their rectum as the "price for curing cancer".
"What these results suggest is that for many people, this price no longer has to be paid," he said.
Patients whose cancer was not completely eradicated by their treatment during the trial had a surgical procedure to remove the remaining areas affected by cancer.
The results showed that for up to 12 months, four out of five patients treated with chemotherapy and radiotherapy avoided major surgery, compared with three out of five treated with radiotherapy alone.
Patients' progress was followed for 30 months. These results are still being analysed, and the longer-term results are expected to be published in 2027.
Michelle Mitchell, Cancer Research UK's chief executive, said: "This breakthrough could be life-changing for thousands of people."
She said thanks to bowel screening, more rectal cancers were being detected at an earlier stage "where people are more likely to survive the disease".
"But that hasn't made treatment any easier - many patients still have to cope with extremely difficult and often life-altering side effects."
summary: A major international trial called STAR-TREC has found that treating early-stage rectal cancer with combinations of chemotherapy and radiotherapy can help many patients avoid major surgery and permanent colostomy bags. Led by the Universities of Leeds and Birmingham, the initial results suggest that organ-preserving treatments are a realistic option that can keep cancer under control. Up to 12 months after treatment, four out of five patients who received chemotherapy and radiotherapy avoided major surgery.
key_points: The STAR-TREC trial was led by the Universities of Leeds and Birmingham and funded by Cancer Research UK.
Findings published in Lancet Oncology showed that organ-preserving treatments can help early-stage rectal cancer patients avoid major surgery like Total Mesorectal Excision.
Up to 12 months into the study, four out of five patients treated with chemotherapy and radiotherapy avoided major surgery, compared to three out of five treated with radiotherapy alone.
Longer-term results following patients for 30 months are currently being analysed and are expected to be published in 2027.

title: Toddler with sun ‘allergy’ no longer has to play in darkness
author: Telegraph Reporters
content:
![Mollie Murray](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000499279273_17875009399540_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqNPUhnktKekiIw5QCPcpjG2QnZJIETfWB_fUbKb77n0w.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Mollie Murray](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000499279273_17875009399540_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqNPUhnktKekiIw5QCPcpjG2QnZJIETfWB_fUbKb77n0w.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
A toddler with a rare genetic disorder that makes her “allergic” to the sun can finally play without the curtains closed after UV-resistant film was installed on windows at her father’s home.
Two-year-old Mollie Murray, of Montrose in Angus, Scotland, is the only child in the UK known to have her specific variant of xeroderma pigmentosum (XP), making her skin extremely sensitive to ultraviolet light.
The genetic condition, which has no cure, puts Mollie at risk of severe sun damage all year round. She can only go outside safely in protective full-length clothing or after dark.
Her mother Kirsty Campbell, a 35-year-old charge nurse, said: “She burns all year round and has burnt in November before.
“The only time it’s safe to go outside is in the dark. I want to keep her inside at all times to keep her safe, but we can’t do that – she needs some sort of normality.
“We initially had to play inside in darkness with the curtains closed before getting the UV-resistant film on our windows.”
![Kirsty Campbell with Molly](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000499279387_17875009544360_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqZgEkZX3M936N5BQK4Va8RWtT0gK_6EfZT336f62EI5U.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Ms Campbell has spoken out to raise awareness of Mollie’s condition and to thank the Archie Foundation for the funding it provided to help Ryan Murray, 34, Mollie’s father, to install the UV-resistant film in July.
“Their support has been indescribable, they’ve been a massive help for us,” said Ms Campbell.
“It means she can do simple things like look outside for the postman or draw in daylight. My ex-partner was having to take play-park equipment into his house as it wasn’t safe outside. She’s so happy running around like a normal child.”
Doctors have said that Mollie is 10,000 times more likely to develop skin cancer than other children, and Ms Campbell has to use a UV monitor to check readings in every room to ensure it is safe for Mollie to go inside.
![Mollie Murray](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000499279368_17875009689400_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqOCKMJrhy56GMaVAaMhDnyWQnZJIETfWB_fUbKb77n0w.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
“To go from thinking your child has sunburn to them having an extremely rare genetic disorder is mind-blowing,” she said.
“Everyday life is difficult as she needs full protective outerwear for going outside and sun cream every two hours under her clothes.”
Mollie’s family are hoping to ensure she has the highest quality of life possible while continuing to keep her safe. Ms Campbell said: “She is an amazing wee girl and is coping with it so well.”
The Archie Foundation provides support to babies, children and families during a hospital stay or after a bereavement.
It gave Mollie’s family £600 to fund UV film for the whole downstairs of her father’s house and her bedroom upstairs, which was installed on July 15.
Rebecca Duncan, the business development manager for the Tayside-based foundation, said: “Caring for a child with complex needs can be incredibly challenging and, at times, isolating, so we’re committed to ensuring families never feel they have to face that journey alone.
“Mollie has shown remarkable resilience. We’re proud to have played a small part in helping her experience the joy, opportunities and precious moments that every child deserves.”
summary: A two-year-old Scottish toddler with a rare genetic disorder that makes her extremely sensitive to ultraviolet light can now play in daylight after UV-resistant film was installed on windows at her father's home. Mollie Murray is the only child in the UK known to have her specific variant of xeroderma pigmentosum, a condition with no cure that increases her risk of severe sun damage and skin cancer. Thanks to £600 in funding from the Archie Foundation, the protective window film allows her to safely look outside and play indoors with the curtains open.
key_points: Two-year-old Mollie Murray is the only child in the UK with her specific variant of xeroderma pigmentosum, an incurable genetic condition causing extreme UV sensitivity.
The Archie Foundation provided £600 to fund UV-resistant window film for Mollie's father's house, allowing her to play indoors in daylight instead of darkness.
Mollie faces a 10,000 times higher risk of developing skin cancer than other children and must wear protective full-length clothing and sun cream when going outside.
Her mother, Kirsty Campbell, uses a UV monitor to check room readings and has spoken out to raise awareness of the condition and thank the foundation for its support.

title: Cancer patient campaigns to scrap VAT on sunscreen
author: Mark Norman
content:
![A young woman with shoulder length blonde hair with a red scar and scar tissue under her right eyelid.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/61a0/live/05c35900-9d57-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
Jessica had most of her lower eyelid removed after being diagnosed with skin cancer
- Published
A Sussex woman is calling on the government to scrap VAT on sunscreen after being diagnosed with skin cancer at the age of 26.
Jessica Zbinden-Webster from Ferring in West Sussex will deliver a petition of almost 100,000 signatures to Downing Street, calling on the government to scrap the 20% VAT charged on sunscreen products.
Diagnosed in 2018 Zbinden-Webster said she wanted the government to axe the tax to make sunscreen "more accessible to more people".
The government says it will "fight cancer on all fronts".
Describing her treatment Zbinden-Webster said the tumour had spread quite deep underneath the surface of her skin.
"So I had that lopped off and then the hole was so big that it couldn't be closed with stitches.
I was warned, you know, you may look a little different for a while and as you can see from the pictures, I did look a little different for a while."
Determined to raise awareness of the disease she says it affects about 20% of the population, but it is avoidable in nine out of 10 cases.
"In a cost-of-living crisis, the poorest are priced out of skin cancer prevention because of the 20% 'cosmetic' tax on sunscreen products. Sunscreen is not 'cosmetic' - it's critical," she said.
![A young woman with shoulder length blonde hair wearing a blue dress.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/c62c/live/b636d0b0-9d56-11f1-aac2-870643eea2ac.jpg)
Jessica said she was "horrified" at what she called the "abysmal" sunscreen and sun safety landscape n the UK.
Zbinden-Webster's says the petition is highlighting that skin cancer is now the most common form of cancer in the UK.
A government spokesperson said: "As part of our 10-year plan to reform the health service, and through a national cancer plan, we will fight cancer on all fronts, from prevention, to diagnosis, treatment, and research.
"High-factor sunscreen is on the NHS prescription list for certain conditions and is already provided VAT free when dispensed by a pharmacist to these patients."
Follow BBC Sussex on Facebook, external, X, external, and Instagram, external, and listen to BBC Radio Sussex on Sounds. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk, or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.
summary: Jessica Zbinden-Webster, a skin cancer survivor from West Sussex, is campaigning to remove the 20% VAT on sunscreen to make protection more accessible during the cost-of-living crisis. She is delivering a petition with nearly 100,000 signatures to Downing Street, arguing that sunscreen is a critical health product rather than a cosmetic. The government responded that it plans to fight cancer across all fronts and noted that high-factor sunscreen is already provided VAT-free on NHS prescriptions for certain conditions.
key_points: Jessica Zbinden-Webster is petitioning the government to remove the 20% VAT on sunscreen.
She was diagnosed with skin cancer in 2018 at the age of 26 and underwent extensive treatment.
The petition has gathered almost 100,000 signatures to be delivered to Downing Street.
The government stated it will fight cancer on all fronts and noted high-factor sunscreen is already VAT-free on certain NHS prescriptions.

title: Boy left on the brink of death after receiving 'disgusting' care in hospital
author: Martha Bolt
content:
A boy suffered a stroke after receiving "disgusting" treatment at a hospital in Sussex, his mother claimed.
Junior Fahr, aged seven, was left on the brink of death after "being left for hours" in an A&E waiting room at Worthing Hospital with a blood clot causing the stroke.
A senior NHS director at the hospital apologised for the "distress" caused, admitting it was a "incredibly frightening" experience and said a review had been launched into what happened.
His mother Evangelynne Brooks, 27, said that Junior had been taken to Worthing Hospital after complaining of pins and needles in the left side of his body on May 12.
  Junior and his mum, Evangelynne Brooks prior to the stroke (Image: Evangelynne Brooks)
After doing "some silly little tests" the doctors sent them home.
On June 25, Junior was rushed back to Worthing hospital after vomiting several times and going limp.
When he reached the emergency room, he was "dead-weight", she said.
By the time he was seen, Junior could not walk or talk.
Ms Brooks said: "They were trying to give him anti-sickness tablets but he couldn't even swallow his own spit."
Junior and his family waited for four hours while he was in a "terrible" condition before Ms Brooks' mother spotted that he looked as though he was having a seizure.
  Junior in hospital after suffering a stroke (Image: NQ staff)
A nurse was alerted, but there were doubts that he was having a stroke, Ms Brooks claimed.
She called the care her son received at Worthing Hospital "disgusting".
She said: "If my mum didn't show up when she did, we would be in a very different situation."
When Junior was finally seen by doctors, he was rushed to an adult ward where he had a brain scan, confirming he had a blood clot that caused his stroke.
Junior was blue lighted from Worthing to Southampton hospital for emergency surgery to have the blood clot removed.
"The drive to Southampton felt like forever," Ms Brooks said.
"I felt like I was dreaming."
After surgery, doctors were adamant that Junior had suffered sufficient brain damage and that he had "no chance of survival" after they failed to remove his breathing tube twice.
Ms Brooks was even given the option to let Junior "pass peacefully in his sleep."
But after 24 hours of slow improvement, Junior's breathing tube was removed and he began breathing on his own.
   (Image: NQ staff)
"It was the first glimpse of hope," Ms Brooks said.
Since then, Junior has come a long way.
Ms Brooks said: "The doctors said he was going to die, that he was going to be brain dead.
"He is currently walking, talking and eating.
"It's a miracle."
Since the incident, Worthing Hospital has apologised to Ms Brooks and has informed her that they are investigating "all aspects" of the care Junior received.
In letter addressed to Ms Brooks, Julie Thomas, Hospital Director of Nursing, said: "I would like to acknowledge how incredibly frightening and distressing this experience was for you and your family."
She added: "We are sincerely sorry for the distress that your son and your family have experienced."
Ms Brooks is keen to spread awareness about paediatric strokes.
She said: "Whilst childhood strokes are rare, they do happen, and before this happened to Junior, I never imagined something like this could happen to my little boy.
"One of the reasons I feel it is so important to raise awareness is that children don’t always show the obvious signs of a stroke that we might expect, and symptoms can sometimes be subtle or difficult to recognise."
Junior's family are now raising money for him on a Go Fund Me page to give him "the future he deserves." You can see the fundraising page HERE
A University Hospitals Sussex spokesperson said: “We extend our sincere apologies to Junior and his family, and fully appreciate how difficult this must have been for them.
"We are investigating Junior’s care so that we can fully understand the circumstances, and try to identify whether there is any learning that could help improve our care in the future.
"We will do all we can to support Junior and his family, listen to their concerns, and talk with them whenever they feel ready to speak with us.”
summary: Seven-year-old Junior Fahr suffered a stroke caused by a blood clot after his mother claims he received poor care and long waiting times at Worthing Hospital in Sussex. Following emergency surgery in Southampton and an initial grim prognosis that he would not survive, Junior has since recovered his ability to walk, talk, and eat. A senior NHS director has apologized for the distress caused and confirmed that a review into the incident has been launched.
key_points: Junior Fahr was initially sent home from Worthing Hospital after reporting pins and needles, only to return weeks later vomiting and limp.
His family experienced a four-hour wait in the emergency room before medical staff recognized he was having a seizure and stroke.
Junior was transferred to Southampton hospital for emergency surgery to remove a blood clot and defied doctors' initial expectations of brain death.
Worthing Hospital issued a sincere apology to the family and launched an investigation into the care provided.

title: Why stomach cancer is often diagnosed too late
author: Esther Intabo
content:
When stomach cancer is suspected, getting the diagnosis right is critical because it determines what treatment is appropriate and helps doctors understand the likely course of the disease.
Stomach cancer remains one of the leading causes of cancer-related deaths worldwide, with men continuing to bear a larger share of the burden.
The latest figures from the International Agency for Research on Cancer show that estimated deaths from stomach cancer among people aged 0 to 85 and above rose about 1.9 percent, from 642,000 in 2024 to 654,000 in 2025.
Men accounted for most of these deaths, with the number increasing from 419,000 in 2024 to 426,000 in 2025. Among women, deaths increased from 223,000 to 229,000 over the same period.
Kenya, too, recorded an increase, with stomach cancer deaths among men rising by 3.7 percent from 565 in 2024 to 586 in 2025. Among women, deaths jumped 3.5 percent from 488 to 505 over the same period.
Dr Joseph Abuodha, a consultant medical oncologist at Aga Khan University Hospital, says the number of deaths from stomach cancer almost reflects the number of new cases.
“The biggest question is why would these numbers come to this much and why would the death rate be high? It's because of predominantly late diagnosis,” he says.
Why it is easy to miss
One of the difficulties with stomach cancer is that some of its symptoms can look like ordinary stomach problems.
“A person may experience abdominal discomfort, bloating, pain or what they describe as ulcer-like symptoms. There may also be increased acidity or dyspepsia, symptoms such as bloating, acidity and abdominal discomfort.”
Other warning signs include darkening of the stool, which may indicate bleeding in the stomach, and early satiety, feeling full after eating much less food than one normally would.
Dr Abuodha gives a simple example. “If someone could comfortably eat a full plate of ugali six months ago but now feels full after half a plate, it could be because the stomach is not expanding as it should,” he explains.
Weight loss despite eating what appears to be an adequate amount of food is another symptom.
He notes none of these symptoms automatically means someone has stomach cancer. Many other stomach conditions can cause similar problems. That is part of what makes the disease difficult to identify early.
“What we find in patients who come to us with a diagnosis of cancer is that most of them will have come to hospital at some point for that diagnosis,” says Dr Abuodha.
The problem is that they may have been treated repeatedly for what appeared to be ordinary stomach problems.
A patient may have persistent pain, dyspepsia or acidity and be treated for ulcers, gastritis or H. pylori. The symptoms may temporarily settle, only to return.
“After a few sessions of treatment, you're not getting better, you need to go for an endoscopy.”
The challenge, he says, very early stomach cancer may have no obvious symptoms.
“A person may have no pain at all or may experience only mild discomfort that does not persist. In some cases, early stomach cancer is discovered while doctors are investigating an unrelated problem.”
For example, someone may undergo a CT scan because of abdominal pain and doctors notice something in the stomach that requires further investigation.
Once symptoms become more pronounced, however, the cancer may already be locally advanced. At that point, he says it may still be possible to cure it, but treatment becomes more difficult especially for those who present with more significant symptoms are more likely to have advanced disease.
“The stomach has an opening at the top, where food enters from the throat, and another at the bottom, where food passes into the intestines,” he explains. “If a cancer develops close to either opening, even a small growth can interfere with the passage of food. A feeling that food is getting blocked or is not passing properly can therefore appear relatively early when the cancer is in these areas.”
Still, this is not where stomach cancer most commonly develops. When it develops in the main part of the stomach, the early symptoms can be much less obvious.
The earliest symptoms that people may notice are often within that broad range of dyspepsia, that is, acidity, bloating and abdominal discomfort.
“The challenge is not simply knowing what stomach cancer looks like. It is recognising when ordinary symptoms have persisted for too long and need a closer look.”
He cautions that if symptoms of gastritis or an ulcer persist despite appropriate treatment, further investigation may be necessary.
“If pain changes or a new symptom appears, such as bleeding, vomiting blood or blood in the stool, the problem should be investigated rather than assumed to be simple gastritis.”
People with chronic H. pylori infection or gastritis should also have follow-up depending on the severity of their symptoms. For someone with chronic ulcers, a change in symptoms or the emergence of a new problem should prompt medical review.
There is, however, no direct association between irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and stomach cancer.
Biggest risk factors
According to Dr Abuodha, the biggest risk factor is age. “The older a person gets, the more likely they are to develop the disease,” he says.
Long-standing dietary and lifestyle preferences also matter. Heavy alcohol use can irritate the stomach lining, while heavy cigarette smoking has also been associated with stomach cancer.
Anecdotal evidence also suggests that very spicy or irritating foods, particularly when consumed frequently, may cause ongoing stomach irritation. H. pylori is another important consideration and is associated with a specific type of stomach cancer.
“There are different types, including the more commonly recognised stomach cancer, as well as lymphoma and sarcoma of the stomach and other less common cancers,” he explains.
However, Dr Abuodha notes that less than five percent have a genetic component. Some genetic syndromes can increase the likelihood of developing stomach cancer, sometimes alongside other cancers.
Still, the majority of people who develop stomach cancer have no family history of the disease.
So why are men more affected? “There are about two men with stomach cancer for every woman. Men tend to have more of these risk factors. They may also respond differently to symptoms,” he says, adding that when men get pain, they don't look for healthcare options easily.
Treatment options
When stomach cancer is suspected, getting the diagnosis right is critical because it determines what treatment is appropriate and helps doctors understand the likely course of the disease.
The gold standard for diagnosis is histology, which involves taking a tissue sample during an endoscopy and examining it.
“None is better” than histology, Dr Abuodha says, explaining that other tests are used alongside it to determine treatment options and prognosis.
“Once stomach cancer has been confirmed, doctors may use a CT scan or PET scan to establish how far the disease has progressed. In some cases, an ultrasound through the endoscopy may also be used, particularly when dealing with small stomach cancers.”
Sometimes scans cannot provide the full picture. In such cases, doctors may perform surgical staging, using cameras inserted into the abdomen to look for signs that the cancer has spread and to take samples of anything suspicious.
For advanced stomach cancer, particularly stage four disease that has progressed after at least one chemotherapy option, an expanded gene panel may be recommended. The information can help guide treatment.
Late diagnosis is not always about a patient ignoring symptoms.
Still, there can also be delays within the healthcare system. Dr Abuodha says patients with suspicious symptoms should be referred quickly to the appropriate level of care. Another challenge is the cost and availability of certain diagnostic tests, including endoscopy.
He stresses that eating a well-balanced diet, eating less processed food and choosing quality food rather than focusing only on quantity are important.
Weight management matters because it affects several metabolic processes in the body. Exercise can also help with metabolism and the processing of sugars and fats while reducing inflammation and potential associations with cancer.
Dr Abuodha also advises caution among people who regularly take very hot or highly spicy meals, particularly if these are accompanied by stomach discomfort. Heavy alcohol use and cigarette smoking should be avoided or significantly reduced.
But not everyone carries the same level of risk. This can include someone who has had ulcers and undergone an endoscopy in which a suspicious lesion was found at the mouth of the stomach.
“Depending on the findings and the individual's circumstances, such patients may need repeat endoscopy every six to 12 months. People with a family history of stomach cancer who have not yet undergone genetic testing may be at risk also.”
summary: Stomach cancer remains a leading cause of global cancer deaths, with rising fatalities disproportionately affecting men. The primary reason for high mortality rates is late diagnosis, as early symptoms often mimic common, benign stomach issues like gastritis or ulcers. Risk factors include aging, smoking, heavy alcohol use, and chronic H. pylori infections, while diagnosis typically relies on endoscopy and histology.
key_points: Global and regional stomach cancer deaths are increasing, with men accounting for the majority of fatalities.
Late diagnosis is the primary driver of high mortality rates because early symptoms resemble ordinary stomach problems like acidity, bloating, and ulcers.
Key risk factors for stomach cancer include advanced age, heavy alcohol consumption, cigarette smoking, and chronic H. pylori infections.
Endoscopy combined with histology is considered the gold standard for accurately diagnosing stomach cancer.

title: We Asked 3 Dietitians to Name the Healthiest Tinned Fish—They All Picked the Same One
author: Lauren Manaker M S; RDN; LD; CLEC
content:
![A person in a kitchen examining two tins of food](<https://www.eatingwell.com/thmb/tg1cV0PPmGbiXqECRlltL2pfZEs=/1500x0/filters:no_upscale():max_bytes(150000):strip_icc()/We-Asked-TK-Dietitians-to-Name-the-Healthiest-Tinned-Fish-They-All-Picked-the-Same-One-0cfb8932ca7045eca26224cffc0c2e19.jpg>) 
Getty Images. EatingWell Design.
- Sardines are rich in omega-3s, protein, phosphorus, calcium, vitamin D and B12, making them highly nutritious.
- Their low mercury levels make them a safe, affordable and shelf-stable seafood option.
- Sardines are a versatile ingredient that can be enjoyed as a topping, flavor-booster or spread.
With more tinned fish options on shelves, choosing the right one can feel tricky. From smoked oysters to every imaginable variety of tuna, the options keep growing. To help you navigate the world of tinned fish, we asked registered dietitians what the healthiest option is—they all said sardines.
Sardines are a nutrient-rich fish, serving as a source of omega-3 fatty acids, protein, vitamin D, vitamin B12, calcium and more. Plus, all of those nutrients are packaged in a shelf-stable tin that costs just a few dollars.
They Are a Source of Omega-3 Fatty Acids
Sardines are a strong source of essential omega-3 fatty acids. “Sardines are particularly impressive when it comes to omega-3 content, providing similar amounts as many types of salmon and more than other popular fish, such as tuna,” shares Amy Brownstein, MS, RDN. A single 3-ounce serving delivers nearly your daily requirement of omega-3 fatty acids. They provide two forms of omega-3 fatty acids, EPA and DHA, which are the long-chain fats your body uses most efficiently to support heart health, combat inflammation and promote healthy brain function.
They Provide Plenty of Calcium
Most people are surprised to learn that the bones in sardines are edible, and you should eat them. That’s because the bones soften during the canning process, making them easy to eat and virtually undetectable in most recipes. “Sardine bones are thin and flavorless and easily dissolve when mashed or incorporated into other dishes,” per Brownstein. And those tiny bones are what supply a significant amount of calcium and phosphorus.
A 3-ounce serving of sardines provides roughly 324 milligrams of calcium, comparable to about a cup of skim milk. That’s a little over one-third of the recommended daily intake for most adults, making sardines a source of calcium for people who can’t eat dairy.phosphorus, which works alongside calcium to support bone strength.
Related Stories
![Exterior view of a ChickfilA restaurant showing logos and building design](<https://www.eatingwell.com/thmb/jZq5EHltaqtYNGWS7pOhuf061a8=/300x200/filters:no_upscale():max_bytes(150000):strip_icc()/We-Asked-4-Dietitians-the-Worst-Order-at-Chick-fil-A-844e7163703740b7b04fa55a703c20f7.jpg>) 
![A person using a toaster in a modern kitchen preparing breakfast](<https://www.eatingwell.com/thmb/qPhY6lM5QSudWZ9KJzE5rKomq18=/300x200/filters:no_upscale():max_bytes(150000):strip_icc()/We-Asked-TK-Chefs-the-Best-Brand-of-Frozen-Waffles-They-All-Picked-the-Same-One-50e0f1b987804ccf8e11897b55a181ae.jpg>) 
They Are Lower in Mercury Than Most Fish
Mercury is a legitimate concern with seafood, but sardines tend to have lower mercury content than other fish. “Their low position on the food chain means they have very low mercury levels, making them safe for pregnant women and children,” shares Whitney Stuart, MS, RDN.
That makes sardines one of the most worry-free oily fish options you can eat regularly. The American Heart Association recommends at least two 3-ounce portions of fish per week, including one serving of oily fish.Jamie Lee McIntyre, MS, RDN.
They Are Rich in Protein and Micronutrients
Beyond omega-3s and calcium, sardines deliver a strong lineup of other essential nutrients. One 3-ounce serving provides 21 grams of protein, which supports muscle maintenance, satiety and overall metabolic function.vitamin D, which is a nutrient many people fall short on.vitamin B12, which plays a key role in nerve function and red blood cell production.iron, potassium, magnesium and zinc, making them one of the more nutritionally complete tinned foods available.
They May Support Heart and Metabolic Health
Sardines can be a key player in promoting both heart and metabolic health. In one 12-month randomized trial, older adults with prediabetes who added about 200 grams (about 7 ounces) of sardines per week to their diet saw improvements in HDL cholesterol, triglycerides, blood pressure and markers of insulin resistance compared with a control group.
Ways to Enjoy Sardines
- Choose sardines packed in water or olive oil. Sauce-packed varieties can be higher in sodium and added sugar, so check the label. If sodium is a concern, rinsing water-packed sardines before eating them can help reduce sodium content.
- On top of toast or crackers. This is the most approachable entry point. Top with a squeeze of lemon, a little Dijon mustard or a drizzle of olive oil and a pinch of red pepper flakes for a delicious, balanced bite.
- Mix into pasta dishes. Break sardines up and fold them into a simple pasta with garlic, olive oil, capers and lemon. They melt into the sauce and add savory depth without overtaking the flavor of the dish.
- Add to a grain bowl. Add sardines to a bowl with farro, quinoa or brown rice, roasted vegetables and a bright vinaigrette. They add protein and healthy fats, making the bowl more satisfying.
- Mash into a spread or dip. Blend sardines with cream cheese or Greek yogurt, lemon juice and fresh herbs for a spread that works on crudités, crackers or as a sandwich filling.
RECIPES TO TRY
![3757396.jpg](<https://www.eatingwell.com/thmb/v8-IxR0fmqtK_MouYf1bhEDIf44=/300x200/filters:no_upscale():max_bytes(150000):strip_icc()/3748010-7d5aebc54b88431c9318a0b9dcf9e593.jpg>) 
![3755591.jpg](<https://www.eatingwell.com/thmb/Vsj9HR49ry7wxMxrZtypqgaACy8=/300x200/filters:no_upscale():max_bytes(150000):strip_icc()/3746227-af886c6f30d3411ba0c6dc96fea56ef8.jpg>) 
![spicy sardine linguine](<https://www.eatingwell.com/thmb/f9ekDRTI0LEQQvb8ciNKpab3kdQ=/300x200/filters:no_upscale():max_bytes(150000):strip_icc()/spicy-sardine-linguine-53a79d37b9d14d6ca0e69602184eeab2.jpg>) 
Our Expert Take
Sardines earn their status as the healthiest tinned fish by being loaded with essential fats, vitamins and minerals. They deliver nutrients like omega-3 fatty acids, high-quality protein, calcium, vitamin D and B12, all in a low-mercury, affordable, shelf-stable package. Eating sardines with the bones adds an extra layer of nutritional value by providing calcium and phosphorus. Whether you’re trying to eat more fish, support your heart health or simply upgrade your pantry staples, sardines are one of the most practical and nutrient-dense options you can reach for.
summary: When asked by editors to name the healthiest tinned fish, registered dietitians unanimously chose sardines. These nutrient-dense fish are rich in omega-3 fatty acids, protein, vitamins D and B12, and calcium from their edible bones. Additionally, sardines are low in mercury, affordable, and shelf-stable, making them a practical and healthy dietary addition.
key_points: Sardines were unanimously named the healthiest tinned fish by consulted registered dietitians.
A single 3-ounce serving provides essential omega-3 fatty acids, 21 grams of protein, and significant amounts of calcium, vitamin D, and vitamin B12.
Because they sit low on the food chain, sardines have low mercury levels, making them safe for regular consumption by pregnant women and children.
The tiny bones in canned sardines soften during processing and are edible, providing a substantial source of calcium and phosphorus.
Sardines are versatile and can be enjoyed on toast, mixed into pasta, added to grain bowls, or blended into spreads.

title: Belfast pain rehabilitation programme at Knockbracken 'gives patients back control'
author: Marie-Louise Connolly
content:
![A woman smiling at the camera. She has long grey hair and is wearing a yellow top and blue jacket.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/ca9f/live/cb4868d0-9d54-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Julie-Ann Walkden had relied on pills and injections to cope with chronic pain
- Published
For years Julie-Ann Walkden had relied on pills and injections to cope with chronic pain, but it was an understanding of what was going on that helped her get her life back.
"I didn't want to take strong medication which made me feel ill, not in control and often so confused that I felt I'd dementia," she said.
She was among more than 100 patients who have completed a pain rehabilitation programme, using exercise, talking and psychological therapies to help them understand the source of their pain.
Walkden was speaking after a new study revealed that people in the most deprived socio-economic areas of Northern Ireland are at higher risk of chronic pain and three times more likely to face pain-related depression.
An intensive programme in Belfast
Ten years ago, Walkden, 58, was prescribed strong pain medication for a long-standing stomach injury, but said it only provided short-term relief and made her feel worse.
However, she found new ways of coping with her condition following a three-week intensive programme at Knockbracken Health Care Park in Belfast, which teaches psychological techniques to deal with pain rather than relying on medication.
"The tools have allowed me to become the boss of the pain instead of it controlling me," she said.
"I am not afraid to exercise, especially to walk, I even talk to the pain but I no longer allow it to prevent me from living a life.
"Understanding the source of my pain and what it is doing to me mentally, never mind physically, has been life changing."
Data collected from the Knockbracken programme has formed part of new research from Queen's University Belfast (QUB) and the Belfast Health Trust.
While more than 100 people within the Belfast Trust physically took part, the study also analysed the data of 491 patients living with chronic pain in Northern Ireland.
It found that 42% of those were living in the most deprived areas and reported much higher levels of distress, disability and pain-related burden.
Researchers 'shocked' by the findings
![A man looking at the camera with brown hair. He is wearing a grey jacket and navy shirt.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/7493/live/c5172c80-9d54-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Professor Kevin Vowles led the study
Professor Kevin Vowles from QUB, who led the study, said: "What we found is that individuals who live in high areas of social deprivation are at substantially increased risk of huge disruptions in social functioning, emotional functioning, physical functioning.
"The degree of that difference is so significant that as researchers and clinicians we were genuinely shocked; we did not expect the result to be as bad as it was.
"We found extremely high levels of anxiety and from a statistical perspective that pattern of findings is hugely unique, hugely unexpected and hugely significant."
According to the study, chronic pain costs the UK Â£10bn annually in healthcare and lost productivity.
'I curled into the foetal position'
Chronic pain is defined as pain that lasts longer than three months and means the nervous system stays stuck in emergency mode.
Learning how it works is the first step toward getting the right care and taking control of your life again.
Frank McCoubrey, a Belfast City Councillor, said his pain ,which was based in his spine, has at times made his life unbearable for more than 15 years.
"Some days I just curled into the foetal position and stayed in bed because the pain was so severe," he said.
"I became frightened of it and how it controlled me, " McCoubrey said.
Like Walkden, medication made McCoubrey feel drowsy, nauseous and caused disturbed sleep.
McCoubrey said he was not shocked to discover that people living in the most deprived areas were more adversely affected by pain than others.
"People in my area talk about how physical pain prevents them from working, exercising and pain can generally just drag you down, " he said.
![A bald man looking at the camera. He has a moustache and is wearing a black and white striped shirt.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/8016/live/ab765a30-9d54-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Cllr Frank McCoubrey has had chronic pain for 15 years
Strategies to manage pain
The study found that depression and anxiety increased proportionally with deprivation levels.
The most deprived group experienced up to three times more pain-related issues with mental health, social functioning, and physical disability, compared to the least deprived.
"There are times I am still in a great deal of pain, but the difference now is I understand it, the source of it and I control it - it doesn't control me," McCoubrey said.
Dr Rory Maguire, a consultant in pain medicine, said the programme marks a change from relying on medication and procedures.
"What we're looking to do by just incorporating physical strategies, psychological strategies, is give them really long-term means to manage pain and to build their life up to have a successful quality of life again," he said.
summary: An intensive three-week pain rehabilitation programme at Knockbracken Health Care Park in Belfast is helping patients manage chronic pain through exercise, talking, and psychological therapies instead of relying on medication. Meanwhile, new research from Queen's University Belfast and the Belfast Health Trust revealed that people in the most deprived socio-economic areas of Northern Ireland face a significantly higher risk of chronic pain and are three times more likely to experience pain-related depression and anxiety. Participants like Julie-Ann Walkden and Belfast City Councillor Frank McCoubrey reported that understanding the source of their pain and learning non-medical coping strategies has allowed them to regain control of their lives.
key_points: More than 100 patients have completed the intensive pain rehabilitation programme at Knockbracken Health Care Park in Belfast.
The programme utilizes exercise, talking, and psychological therapies to help patients manage chronic pain instead of relying heavily on medication.

A study by Queen's University Belfast and the Belfast Health Trust found that individuals in the most deprived areas are at a substantially increased risk of chronic pain and severe disruptions in functioning.
Researchers were shocked to discover that people in the most deprived socio-economic areas are three times more likely to face pain-related depression and anxiety.
Chronic pain costs the UK £10bn annually in healthcare and lost productivity.

title: Doctors wrongly said I was too young to have endometriosis at 13
author: Vicki Loader
content:
![The young women has long, blonde hair falling over her right shoulder. She is wearing a blue dress with thin straps and gold hoop earrings. She has tanned skin and blue eyes and is looking straight into the camera with a closed-mouth smile.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/b09c/live/25655b50-9b04-11f1-bb80-c1b1e1adeea5.jpg)
Grace struggled with severe period pain before she was diagnosed with endometriosis
- Published
Every month, at about the time of her period, Grace has to be taken to hospital.
She is often in so much pain her parents have to carry her to the car. She can wait hours to be seen in A&E, only to be sent home in tears with more strong painkillers.
For a long time, Grace - who's now 14 and is from Yorkshire - felt doctors were dismissive of her pain. "I feel like I was seen as a girl who didn't want to go to school and was being dramatic," she says.
She was given multiple possible reasons for her symptoms: irritable bowel syndrome, a cyst, anxiety and "just a bad period". But, she says, "I knew it was more than that."
Doctors told her time and again that it could not be endometriosis - an incurable condition causing lesions and scarring on internal organs and around the body, external - because she was too young. Grace says her requests for further investigation were ignored.
'It's like heated barbed wire around my abdomen'
Grace's periods began when she was 11, and by 13, she was having excruciating pains around the time of menstruation. She describes it as if "heated barbed wire" were wrapped around her abdomen: "It's like my organs are being pulled apart."
She is often bedbound and, whenever she has exhausted the painkillers she has at home, she has to go in to hospital, where she is regularly given morphine. She has also been given co-codamol and tramadol.
Dependency on strong drugs like opioids worries her. "It's scary," she says, "because I don't want to have to rely on them for the rest of my life."
![A young woman is lying in a hospital bed wearing a hospital gown and partly covered by a white sheet. We can't see her face as it is hidden by the bed arm. She seems like she may be asleep.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1056/cpsprodpb/4000/live/c188f250-9b07-11f1-bb80-c1b1e1adeea5.jpg)
Grace has been hospitalised and regularly given opiods like morphine for her pain
But the most frustrating thing for Grace, and why she contacted BBC Your Voice, is because she does not feel medical experts recognise that teenagers and adolescents can suffer from endometriosis.
Grace's GP did not diagnose her condition and nor did the first consultant she saw privately.
She says: "Even a specialist didn't believe me. And if a specialist won't listen to me, who will?" It was not until the family pushed for a second private opinion that she got a positive diagnosis.
Endometriosis, which occurs when tissue similar to the lining of the womb grows outside it, can cause debilitating symptoms, such as pelvic pain, heavy periods and fatigue. About 10% of women are affected by it, according to NHS data.
It can develop at any age once periods begin - and it is a common misconception that only older women suffer from the condition, says the charity Endometriosis UK,
Faye Farthing, a spokesperson for the charity, says the government, NHS and health practitioners need to improve menstrual health education for young people "if we are to ensure the next generation are not robbed of the future they deserve".
The charity says it can take a long time to diagnose endometriosis - an average of nine years in older women.
And in the early stages, for example with teenagers, it often doesn't show up on an ultrasound scan. However, new tests are being developed which will help spot the condition earlier.
Getting pregnant can be more difficult - even aged 14, Grace says she has been warned it is likely to affect her fertility. She's been advised she may not be able to have children after the age of 30 because of damage to her reproductive organs.
She feels rushed: "I have to have kids within the next 15 years, otherwise I might not be able to."
![A young woman poses centered against a vibrant, pop-art style backdrop with bright yellow burst patterns and comic-book style red and black arrows or stars pointing inward.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/713/cpsprodpb/5132/live/a22f4800-9b07-11f1-bb80-c1b1e1adeea5.jpg)
Grace now has a diagnosis of endometriosis and is having treatment to ease her condition
Paediatric gynaecologist Dr Gail Busby says nearly 80% of adolescents will have painful periods, but clinicians should recognise when a patient's symptoms are not normal - like missing school, missing PE every month or not going out with friends.
She says: "When you're in bed and your best friend is a hot water bottle - that's not normal."
Grace's case, showing symptoms at the age of 13, is not unusual, says Dr Busby, who sees girls both younger and older than Grace at her clinics. As well as her NHS work, she has opened a private adolescent endometriosis clinic in Manchester.
The impact of symptoms is not just physical. Girls like Grace are more likely to suffer with anxiety or depression because their pain affects what is an important time for educational, emotional and social development.
"We should enjoy adolescence," Dr Busby says, "but they can't do what they enjoy doing, what their peers are enjoying doing."
There is a history of endometriosis in Grace's family, but her mum Samantha says that did not make it any easier to get a diagnosis.
"When your child's on the floor in pain, it's very clear it's not just a bad period. But professionals say 'Oh we'll just put you on the pill for six months and see see how we go.'"
Grace has recently had a laparoscopy - keyhole surgery - to remove her endometriosis.
She hopes the procedure will help relieve her symptoms, at least temporarily. She has been advised to take a hormonal contraceptive to help slow monthly tissue growth and lessen the pain.
By speaking out, Grace hopes more teenagers will have the confidence to pursue a diagnosis. "I felt I was going crazy. That it was all in my head," she says. "But actually, you know your body best and your pain is real."
![Your Voice banner image. Your Voice is written in white against a purple background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1376/cpsprodpb/4210/live/7511e550-8aca-11f1-b2ab-0dd01740f9f6.png)
  - Published1 June
 ![A composite image of three women who all have endometriosis: in the centre is the BBC's Emma Barnett, who has long blonde hair and wears tortoiseshell glaasses and a blue top. On the left, is Madalitso, a woman with a streak of pink in her hair, and a purple padded jacket over a fuchsia top. On the right is Chloe, who has red hair and wears a denim jacket.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/840f/live/8359ef10-5b70-11f1-8b8c-6d33e1d5abb6.jpg)
- ![A woman lies on a sofa at home in visible discomfort with her arms on her stomach.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/a852/live/6c3989f0-4462-11f1-ac78-2112837ce2aa.jpg)
- ![Ami Robertson sits in a Pilates studio. She is holding a dog on her lap and is smiling at the camera. She has long blonde hair.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/605/cpsprodpb/6cd6/live/77afef50-79e0-11f1-a400-b302bc872d47.jpg)
summary: Grace, a 14-year-old from Yorkshire, struggled with severe period pain and was repeatedly told by doctors that she was too young to have endometriosis. After facing dismissive medical responses and relying heavily on strong painkillers and hospital visits, her family eventually secured a positive diagnosis through a second private opinion. She hopes speaking out will help other teenagers trust their bodies and pursue timely diagnoses.
key_points: Grace experienced excruciating menstrual pain starting at age 13, leading to frequent hospitalizations and reliance on strong opioids like morphine.
Initial doctors and a private consultant dismissed her symptoms, claiming she was too young for endometriosis and misdiagnosing her with issues like IBS or anxiety.
Charity Endometriosis UK notes that the condition can develop at any age once periods begin and that a common misconception exists that only older women suffer from it.
Grace has since undergone a laparoscopy to remove endometriosis tissue and has been advised to use hormonal contraceptives to manage future pain and fertility concerns.

title: Eight-year-old dies after contracting rare brain-eating amoeba in Louisiana
author: Marina Dunbar
content:
An eight-year-old Louisiana girl has died after contracting a rare, typically fatal brain-eating amoeba after a swim in Lake Claiborne.
Lillian Smart, of Ruston, died on Saturday, one day after celebrating her birthday, her family announced in a public Facebook post on the “Love for Lillian” page.
“Last night Lillian ran from our arms to the arms of Jesus,” her family said in the post. “The injuries to her brain were too severe for her little body to recover from. Everyone did everything they could to keep her here. We are heartbroken and honestly do not know what to do next. How do we put one foot in front of the other without our girl?”
The Louisiana department of health confirmed on 19 August that a state resident had been infected with Naegleria fowleri and said the exposure most likely occurred while the person was swimming in Lake Claiborne in Claiborne parish. Family friends later identified Lillian as the infected resident, according to reports from several local media outlets.
![photomicrograph of green circles](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/019239524ac43d119e139a0d7381e70dc50b87e0/0_0_2932_2021/master/2932.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Naegleria fowleri infections are almost always fatal.
Lillian had been hospitalized since 15 August, KNOE reported. As her family faced the crisis, more than two dozen businesses in Ruston showed support and donated a portion of sales to the Smart family, according to the Facebook page.
Naegleria fowleri infections are extremely rare, with only a handful occurring in Louisiana since 2011.
The amoeba flourishes in warm water and is most commonly found in southern states during the summer. Only about 180 cases have been identified in the US since 1937, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
In 2023, an Arkansas child died after contracting Naegleria fowleri from a country club splash pad in the state capital of Little Rock.
Naegleria fowleri can be found in warm freshwater across the country, including lakes, rivers and ponds. It is not found in salt water or in swimming pools that are properly maintained and chlorinated.
Experts say the climate crisis is causing the amoeba to pop up in parts of the US where it isn’t typical, such as the north and west. It is likely to cause primary amebic meningoencephalitis, a brain infection that can develop when contaminated water enters the nose and the amoeba travels to the brain.
People cannot become infected just by swallowing water containing Naegleria fowleri, and the infection does not spread from one person to another.
summary: An eight-year-old Louisiana girl named Lillian Smart has died from a rare brain-eating amoeba infection after swimming in Lake Claiborne. The infection, caused by Naegleria fowleri, is almost always fatal and typically occurs through exposure to warm freshwater. State health officials and family confirmed the diagnosis following her hospitalization.
key_points: Lillian Smart died from a Naegleria fowleri infection after swimming in Lake Claiborne.
The Louisiana department of health confirmed the infection on August 19, stating exposure likely happened in Lake Claiborne.
Naegleria fowleri infections are extremely rare, highly fatal, and flourish in warm freshwater.
Infection occurs when contaminated water enters the nose and travels to the brain; it cannot be contracted by swallowing water or from person-to-person contact.

title: A gut health scientist easily eats 50 grams of fiber a day. Here's her breakfast, lunch, and dinner.
author: Kim Schewitz
content:
Megan Rossi is serious about fiber.
The dietitian and gut health scientist based at King's College London estimates that she eats between 50 and 60 grams of the hearty stuff every day.
"It sounds like a lot, but our ancestors used to have 100 grams of fiber a day," Rossi told Business Insider.
Fiber is found in plant foods like fruits and veggies, whole grains, beans, nuts, and seeds. It plays many crucial roles in the body, including feeding the trillions of "good" microbes living in the colon lining, which make up part of the gut microbiome and influence overall health.
"Fiber is beneficial because it doesn't feed the human part of us. It feeds the bacterial part of us. And when the bacteria eat the fiber, they produce all these amazing chemicals which help things like our mental health, keep our gut lining strong, regulate our appetite, our hormone balance," Rossi said.
Although the dietary guideline in the UK, where Rossi lives, is 30 grams of fiber daily, she aims for 50 grams because evidence suggests this amount could improve mood, although more research is needed.
As awareness of fiber's role in balancing blood sugar, supporting the gut microbiome, and helping prevent chronic diseases, including colon cancer, has risen, fiber-maxxing — increasing how much fiber you eat — has taken off online. But experts have long encouraged people to eat more fiber, gradually increasing the amounts to help prevent bloating, gas, and abdominal pain.
Rossi doesn't find it difficult to achieve her goal. "It's not that hard if you're thinking every meal, 'OK, where am I getting my fiber from?'" she said.
Here's how she packs 50 grams of fiber into her day.
Fiber-maxxing at breakfast
Rossi's breakfast typically contains around 18 grams of fiber. She regularly makes fermented overnight oats, which involves soaking oats in kefir, a fermented milk drink that contains live bacteria, instead of regular milk.
"What happens is, the bacteria start to ferment it down, and actually produce organic acids and beneficial chemicals," she said of the kefir-soaked oats.
She recommends adding mixed seeds, carrot, mashed banana, and walnuts to the oat mix.
Super Six for lunch
Lunch is typically a "throw-together bowl," containing at least one of the six different plant-based food groups, or what Rossi calls "the Super Six""
- Fruit
- Veggies
- Legumes, such as beans or chickpeas
- Wholegrains, such as bulgur wheat or oats
- Nuts and seeds
- Herbs and spices
Once a week, Rossi preps a batch of cooked mixed grains like quinoa and buckwheat. A typical lunch bowl will contain the prepped grains, canned beans, nuts and seeds, a drizzle of extra virgin olive oil and balsamic vinegar, and a dollop of yogurt.
A fiber-packed smoothie break
As an afternoon snack, Rossi makes a fruit and vegetable-forward smoothie, which "is a really easy way to get an extra 10 grams of fiber, if not more," she said.
She leans heavily on frozen produce, often using cauliflower, berries, kale, mango, or pineapple, and always includes some fresh cucumber and carrot. She also adds yogurt or kefir, some regular milk, and a bit of oat milk.
To balance out the higher sugar content of the fruit, Rossi makes sure she adds two vegetables for every one type of fruit, she said.
A simple stir-fry for dinner
Rossi typically has a stir-fry for dinner. To keep things interesting, she changes up the seasoning by using different herbs, spices, and sauces.
"You just change the flavors, have oregano instead of smoky paprika," she said.
The stir-fry base is always a protein source, plus mixed vegetables and a legume, she said.
After dinner, Rossi likes to have frozen berries with kefir as a sweet treat. "I kind of whip it together like a little ice cream," she said.
summary: Gut health scientist and dietitian Megan Rossi consumes between 50 and 60 grams of fiber daily to support her gut microbiome and overall health. She easily achieves this intake by incorporating plant-based foods, whole grains, beans, nuts, and seeds into every meal. Her daily routine includes fermented overnight oats for breakfast, a grain-and-bean bowl for lunch, a vegetable-heavy smoothie for a snack, and a stir-fry for dinner.
key_points: Megan Rossi aims for 50 to 60 grams of fiber per day, exceeding the UK dietary guideline of 30 grams.
Her breakfast typically features fermented overnight oats soaked in kefir, mixed seeds, carrot, banana, and walnuts, providing about 18 grams of fiber.
Lunch usually consists of a throw-together bowl containing items from her 'Super Six' plant-based food groups.
Her afternoon snack is a fruit and vegetable smoothie using a ratio of two vegetables for every one fruit.
Dinner is typically a customizable stir-fry built on a protein source, mixed vegetables, and legumes.

title: A split in the spectrum? The ongoing battle to define autism
author: Catherine Burns
content:
A split in the spectrum? The ongoing battle to define autism
![BBC A paper cut-out showing a woman's head shrinking within larger cut-outs](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/37a5/live/985111b0-9ca6-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg.webp) BBC
If someone asked you to think of an autistic person, who would come to mind?
The world's richest man, Elon Musk?
Maybe Greta Thunberg, who says being different can be a superpower.
Or Robbie Williams, who has recently revealed he's found out that he has "a bit of autism".
What about someone like 34-year old James Fitzpatrick? He doesn't talk, has a learning disability and needs constant care.
A diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) means someone has certain core characteristics including differences in how they communicate and behave. It's an umbrella term that includes people with very different experiences.
