In recent years there has been an explosion in the number of people with an autism diagnosis on their GP record. In England, it has gone from just over 700,000 three years ago to around 1.1 million today.
The National Autistic Society (NAS) says "evidence suggests there is a significant underdiagnosis of autism, particularly among women and older people".
But what if some people with a diagnosis aren't actually autistic? What if they've really been misdiagnosed?
These questions largely come from 85-year-old Professor Dame Uta Frith - one of the key figures in autism research since the 1960s.
They go to the heart of a debate that is central to the identity of many autistic people.
![Reuters Greta Thunberg wearing a white t-shirt and patterned scarf. She is photographed while talking](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/7225/live/3c585750-9ca7-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg.webp) Reuters
Dame Uta says this is about misdiagnosis - people wrongly being told they are autistic.
She is reluctant to say how many people she thinks have wrongly told they have autism: "In my worst moments, I think it's a great number, but in my best moments, I think it is a small number."
Dame Uta is worried that autistic people who need a lot of support are not getting the help they need.
Some autism researchers and charities say her views are "dangerous", "misinformation" and pit "autistic people against each other". Many autistic people are angry too, saying this calls their identity and rights into question.
The increase in diagnoses of neurodivergent conditions such as autism and ADHD, along with a steep rise in people reporting poor mental health, has prompted a government-commissioned independent review that is due to be published shortly.
But whatever its findings, it is unlikely to be the final word on a question that affects so many people: what actually is autism? And does it matter if such a broad spectrum of people are defined as having it?
Shifting meanings
The definition of autism has shifted and evolved since it was coined in 1911. Then, it was described as a symptom of schizophrenia - excessive fantasies and hallucinations.
By 1943, autism was used to describe children with "fascinating peculiarities" who weren't interested in the world around them.
In the 1960s, it was estimated that 0.04% of children were autistic and most had intellectual disabilities.
By the early 1980s, researchers embraced the idea of an autism spectrum, arguing that autistic people could have average - or very high - intelligence.
This new category of autism was known as Asperger's Syndrome after a little-known paper dating back to Austria in the 1940s, but the term is no longer used.
In 2013, ASD became the official diagnosis for all autistic people. But some autism experts think this is too broad.
Dame Uta ignited this debate by arguing that the autistic spectrum has come to its collapse because people included in it have such different needs.
Questioning the spectrum
A quick search through social media tells you that the 85-year-old is "a pioneer", "brilliant" and the "grand dame of autism research".
But also, a "traitor", an "out-of-touch grifter" who is "past her sell-by date".
During one of our conversations, she receives an email - hate mail. It tells her she will have blood on her hands and contains expletives.
She says: "Some people would say it would be better for me to stop. But I want to get at the truth."
But, even so, she hesitated for years before speaking out, partly because she "really, really" doesn't want to hurt people.
She talks about being driven by "almost a duty" to represent autistic people with intellectual disabilities. She thinks they are being ignored "both in research and in general awareness".
About a third of autistic people have intellectual disabilities. But they are underrepresented in research - a 2019 study found that they make up about 6% of research participants.
Dame Uta says: "These cases are in great need of support. They have been completely overshadowed."
She would include this group on a "pruned" autism spectrum along with people who have what used to be known as Asperger's and autistic people who are diagnosed during childhood.
![Getty Images Hans Asperger standing up at a conference. He wears a light suit and is surrounded by other delegates. The photograph is black and white](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/9ead/live/48c8b2a0-9ca7-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg.webp) Getty Images
She thinks the rise in autism diagnoses is driven by a "late-diagnosed group, mainly females".
The NHS says it can be difficult to recognise autism in women, but Dame Uta says: "I am sceptical of late diagnosis. That's where I think the diagnostic process has become very superficial."
She believes many of this group actually have other conditions including anxiety, depression or OCD.
She questions: "Are they best served by this label autism? I would like them to get better service than they're getting."
She also thinks researchers might need to create "a label that doesn't exist yet" for some people who've been told they're autistic.
She points to research from the University of Cambridge which found that people diagnosed with autism in early childhood often have a different genetic profile to people diagnosed when they are older. Researchers found that people diagnosed when they are older (from late childhood onwards) show an underlying genetic profile that has more in common with ADHD and depression than it does with early diagnosed autism.
But the lead researcher, Dr Varun Warrier, says this shows "autism broadening out genetically" rather than misdiagnosis.
Dame Uta thinks a small number don't have any mental health conditions at all - but are "identity seekers" who have been influenced by bad information on social media.
She hasn't got a number for how many people she thinks have been misdiagnosed, but believes researchers could figure it out.
She knows this will upset and possibly scare people. She stresses: "If someone has been misdiagnosed, I don't want them to suffer for it.
"It would be a terrible thing to take away a diagnosis retrospectively. It's the future I'm concerned with, making diagnostic process more precise - targeting very different individual needs rather than a label."
Culture wars
Dame Uta first expressed her views in an interview with the Times Educational Supplement in March. The NAS reacted to it in strong terms.
It wrote a blog post about "false narratives and outdated ideas", "misinformation" and "false claims".
Dame Uta says it's "just wrong" to dismiss her like this.
The NAS says anyone with an autism diagnosis will have been assessed against strict criteria and "have lifelong differences in communication, behaviours and focused interests compared to non-autistic people".
Dr Sue Smith, the NAS's head of clinical services, says: "We've got a group of people with a genuine need. We're having this weird debate about what they should be called."
She says this isn't just an academic row but has real implications for autistic people: "Historically a lot of people who weren't properly identified as autistic were given other really unhelpful labels", such as borderline personality disorder or bipolar.
She worries that re-labelling some autistic people could lead to them losing support.
Dr Monique Botha, an associate professor of psychology at Durham University, criticised Dame Uta's opinion using swear words.
Botha is autistic and stands by her reaction: "A lot of people were understandably upset and angry… I still am.
"Researchers have a duty to be a bit more blunt and upfront about how damaging these kinds of things can be."
Botha feels that Dame Uta's ideas add to a narrative that "there's some magical easy autism where you're just quirky, where everything in your life will eventually work out, and you're just using this as a crutch so that you can feel special, and it trivialises the reality of a whole bunch of people".
Botha says autistic people are united by key features: sensory sensitivity, a need for predictability, intense interests and struggles with communication.
"That doesn't mean that we will have the same lives or the same outcomes."
James Fitzpatrick was diagnosed in the 1990s, and doesn't speak. His father, Dr Michael Fitzpatrick, is a retired GP.
![Supplied Michael and James Fitzpatrick sit on a sofa together. Michael wears a grey shirt and dark trousers, and james wears a red Batman t-shirt and dark tracksuit bottoms](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/0389/live/5c3dc6e0-9ca7-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg.webp) Supplied
Michael says he's been shocked by the response to Dame Uta's stance: "Intolerant, strident, abusive discourse that's very redolent of the culture wars."
He feels some autistic people don't understand the reality for his family.
Michael says that James, now 34, has "never developed the capacity to engage with the world. That's the source of profound sadness to his family and a loss to himself."
"He would injure himself, bang his head on the floor, bite himself. If you tried to stop him, he would also bite you or scratch you or headbutt you. And as he got bigger, that became more of a problem."
James has calmed down with age but still can "attack you randomly for no apparent reason".
Michael can't see how the same diagnosis can hold true for James and for someone who lives independently - two "extremely different types of people".
Different challenges
Dr Rachel Moseley, an academic from Bournemouth University, was working in autism research when she was diagnosed in her late 20s.
She agrees that people like James are "incredibly neglected".
But she says: "There's room for all of us, we can still advocate for people with learning disabilities without saying that this group isn't valid."
She thinks ideas about dividing up the autistic spectrum lack nuance, especially around mental health.
"Every so often something will totally knock my feet out from under me," Moseley adds, saying she will self-harm and have suicidal thoughts.
"Everyone's challenges are different. But you can't make the assumption that the person with high support needs is always having a harder time. They will in some regards, but not in all."
To make her point, she cites studies that have found that while autistic people overall are more likely to take their own lives, these rates are highest in autistic people without learning disabilities.
Michael Fitzpatrick is unconvinced by this argument: "I seriously, seriously doubt whether the people with autism and no levels of learning disability have a similar level of pathology and life-threatening problems as the people with profound autism."
Lived experience
It's striking that both sides in this row accuse the other of lacking scientific rigour. One major flashpoint is around the study of masking.
This is when someone hides autistic behaviours to try to fit in with society. There's been an explosion of academic interest in this area.
Recently, a review found almost 400 research papers talking about masking, mostly focusing on autistic women who were diagnosed as adults and don't have any intellectual disabilities.
Dame Uta shudders when I mention the idea: "Agh! Such a vague notion." She dismisses some research papers on it as "absolutely poor quality".
Moseley says the exact opposite: "There is really high-quality work on masking, and it's startling and upsetting to see such work be denigrated."
She sees masking research as part of a "refreshing change" as autistic academics "bring lived experience into research".
But Dame Uta questions if autistic researchers can be neutral or if they have a conflict of interest.
![Professor Dame Uta Frith standing in front of a river. She has short grey hair, glasses, pearls and is wearing a dark coat](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/6033/live/c0aa81a0-9ca6-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg.webp)
She's something of an outlier with this view.
Professor Sir Simon Baron-Cohen is director of the Autism Research Centre at the University of Cambridge. When he started out, Dame Uta was his mentor. He disagrees with her on this.
He says: "Someone who's got a degree in molecular biology has one kind of expertise, but someone who's got lived experience has got another kind."
Overall though, Sir Simon says: "I'm not taking sides. I think the answer is to get both sides round the table. A lot of what seem to be irreconcilable differences are actually reconcilable."
He does think the term autism is too broad and can lead to "lumping together people who are so different".
His suggestion is to add sub groups. Type one could be autism with a learning disability. Type two could be autism with language needs. Other types could include conditions that can co-occur with autism, such as ADHD, depression and epilepsy.
He says: "Imagine, we could have dozens or hundreds of subtypes. Why put a limit on it? The more we have, the more precise we can be about what people need."
Once again, there is no consensus.
Dame Uta thinks subtypes could provide "a clean division between those who have these very severe needs and those who don't. But it can't go on endlessly."
The NAS is worried that breaking autism into smaller groups could lead to discrimination or the removal of support from people who need it. It says subtypes have "no clinical value, diagnostic relevance or practical application".
Sir Simon's answer is to "bring in autistic people so we can choose labels that they're comfortable with".
Moving goalposts
Kayleigh was diagnosed with autism in her thirties. She finds that people hold pre-conceived ideas about what autism is.
She explains: "Some will assume you can't spell your own name. Or you love trains. Or you're extremely clever. Or you're hyper focused on a boring hobby."
Since diagnosis she's been given various labels - Asperger's, high-functioning and AuDHD [Autistic with ADHD].
She says: "The goalposts keep moving. As an autistic person, I don't even know what I should be called."
For her, this row is a huge distraction from the real issues.
She's spent her life thinking she was "weird, sub-normal or really, really bad". She's angry that society didn't recognise that she was struggling.
Since diagnosis, she says she's had "zero" support from professionals. She says emotionally she feels she can only really go out if her family are with her. She's not been to her local town centre in years.
She wants more help, more understanding. She doesn't care what her condition is called.
She says: "You could call it 'silly brain disease'. I still know what I'm going through."
Additional reporting by Kris Bramwell
Lead image: Getty
Correction 22 August: This article originally said autism was described in 1911 as a symptom of childhood schizophrenia. The article has been corrected to say that it was described as a symptom of schizophrenia generally.

They are set on an oatmeal, curved background with a green overlapping circle.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/23c7/live/fdf6e630-5e7f-11f1-8b8c-6d33e1d5abb6.png.webp)

summary: Professor Dame Uta Frith has sparked an intense debate by arguing that the modern autism spectrum has become too broad and that many individuals, particularly late-diagnosed women, may be misdiagnosed. While she and supporters argue that high-support needs individuals with intellectual disabilities are being overshadowed, critics and charities contend her views are dangerous, invalidate autistic identities, and risk stripping people of vital support. The controversy highlights ongoing disagreements within the scientific and autistic communities regarding definitions, diagnoses, and the diverse needs of people on the spectrum.
key_points: Autism diagnoses have risen significantly in recent years, growing from just over 700,000 three years ago to around 1.1 million in England.
Professor Dame Uta Frith argues that the autism spectrum has collapsed because it encompasses people with vastly different needs, warning that those requiring high support are being ignored.
Critics from various autism charities and academia have strongly condemned Dame Uta's views as harmful misinformation that pits autistic groups against one another and invalidates late diagnoses.
Debates persist around whether late-diagnosed individuals—especially women—genuinely have autism or might instead be experiencing conditions like anxiety, depression, or OCD.

title: Bristol meningitis survivor feels 'unstoppable' running UK length
author: Leigh Boobyer; Beth Cruse; Georgia Eadie
content:
![Seven runners are lined up on a pavement and smiling for a photo.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/0ee7/live/a9daf7c0-9f17-11f1-b2a2-8945a27a2843.jpg)
Jack Stewart (third from right) is running the length of the UK in 30 days for Meningitis Research Foundation
- Published
A man who is running the length of the UK within 30 days after nearly dying from meningitis as a teenager says he feels "unstoppable."
Jack Stewart, from Bristol, is currently running the equivalent of an ultra marathon - every day from John O' Groats, in Scotland, to Land's End in Cornwall to raise money for Meningitis Research Foundation.
The 30-year-old was initially misdiagnosed with a virus as a 14-year-old in 2009, and a day later his symptoms worsened and he nearly died from meningitis.
"It's been so overwhelming," said Jack's mum, Shelly. "It's just brought a lot of emotion back from 16 years ago and the support is just unbelievable."
Shelly said Jack was sent home ill from school one day in 2009, with symptoms including "feeling delirious, vomiting and not wanting the light on."
Doctors told Shelly Jack had a virus but a day later, Jack was rushed to Bristol Children's Hospital where he was diagnosed with meningitis.
"They told us it would be a 24-hour fight between meningitis and the medication that they've given him and they said it's basically who wins," Shelly said.
![A woman with white hair in a bob wearing black sunglasses and a purple t-shirt is smiling on a summers day.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/0475/live/38dd5b00-9f10-11f1-bca9-4d339be997b1.jpg)
Shelly said the support Jack has received has been "overwhelming"
Jack survived without any after-effects and recovered fully, but had another scare in January after a trip to Sri Lanka to celebrate his 30th birthday.
"It was looking very likely it was meningitis again so of course my world completely collapsed again," she said.
Six days later, doctors confirmed Jack had dengue fever, and not meningitis.
"That's where all this started," she added.
"From his hospital bed he said the NHS have saved me again, I'm going to do something really extraordinary."
'Unstoppable now'
Jack's total journey is about 932 miles (1,500km) and he reached day 24 of 30 on Sunday, running from Gloucester and through his hometown of Bristol.
He has so far raised more than Â£9,000 to go towards research, support and awareness of meningitis.
"I've spent a lot of time on the road on my own so, up north was a real battle," he said.
"I think going through those extreme lows up there on my own and still being able to push through has made me feel like I'm unstoppable now."
On Sunday Jack will run from Bristol to Burnham-on-Sea, in Somerset.
"I feel like what I've been through already there ain't no stopping me now.
"Ive found some purpose here in the last few weeks, I feel like the real Jack is back."
Meningitis - are vaccines available?
![An infographic titled âWhat are the signs of meningitis?â listing symptoms that can appear suddenly and in any order. It includes illustrations for: fever shown with a thermometer; vomiting depicted by a person leaning forward; severe headache shown with red lines around the head; a rash on an arm; a stiff neck illustrated by someone touching their neck; dislike of bright lights shown with an eye shielded by a dark band; drowsiness or difficulty waking shown with a person resting a head on a hand; and seizures illustrated by a figure lying on their side. Text at the bottom notes: âYou do not always get all the symptoms.â Sources: NHS, CDC](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/e9af/live/5f334e10-9ef5-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.png)
The MenACWY vaccine, which is free on the NHS, offers protection against four types of bacteria that can cause meningitis - meningococcal groups A, C, W and Y - and is offered to teenagers aged 14 years old. Anyone who missed out can get it for free until their 25th birthday.
The MenB vaccine helps protect against meningococcal group B bacteria and is recommended for babies aged eight weeks, followed by a second dose at 12 weeks and a booster at one year.
Currently, anyone aged 15 or over can only get a MenB vaccine privately.
However a one-off summer vaccination programme is taking place in the UK to help protect a million young people leaving for university against MenB.
In July, UK experts recommended all teenagers should be offered a free MenB vaccine at about the age of 15 to the government - a change in their previous advice.
summary: Jack Stewart, a 30-year-old meningitis survivor from Bristol, is running the length of the UK from John O'Groats to Land's End in 30 days. He is undertaking the ultra-marathon daily challenge to raise money for the Meningitis Research Foundation after nearly dying from the disease as a teenager and experiencing another meningitis scare in January. Having reached day 24 of his 932-mile journey, he has raised over £9,000 and stated that completing the physical feat makes him feel "unstoppable."
key_points: Jack Stewart is running the length of the UK in 30 days to raise funds for the Meningitis Research Foundation.
Stewart nearly died from meningitis in 2009 at age 14 after initially being misdiagnosed with a virus.
He was inspired to take on the challenge after a health scare in January turned out to be dengue fever rather than a second bout of meningitis.
His roughly 932-mile journey has raised more than £9,000 for meningitis research, support, and awareness.

title: NHS prostate screening limited to just 1,500 men
author: Laura Donnelly
content:
![Actor Colin McFarlane, whose prostate cancer was caught early through screening, took part in an awareness campaign for testing](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000497036564_17875022765430_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqiMxc5qUdCFqatIlsqmFP01HmPOpeFd0SyQx9dn7kM_w.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Actor Colin McFarlane, whose prostate cancer was caught early through screening, took part in an awareness campaign for testing](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000497036564_17875022765430_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqiMxc5qUdCFqatIlsqmFP01HmPOpeFd0SyQx9dn7kM_w.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Just 1,500 men in England are to be offered prostate cancer screening, The Telegraph can disclose.
In May, health chiefs announced plans to screen men with a BRCA2 gene variant and a family history of related cancers.
Around 13,000 men in England aged 45 to 61 are estimated to carry a BRCA2 variant, which can increase the risk of aggressive prostate cancer up to seven-fold.
![A scan makes prostate cancer cells 'glow', reducing the need for invasive biopsies](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000471137451_17875023204890_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqzMzojzwVX9SBGhgJ0n-GXxScrtblwDOyX7sgU0kzxHI.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
However, most men have never undergone genetic testing and would have no reason to know they carry it.
It means that when the programme begins next year, invitations will only go to around 1,500 men who are already known to carry a faulty version of the gene.
Officials have no plans to seek out thousands more who unknowingly carry a BRCA2 variant.
Experts said the approach defied logic, comparing it to “launching a search party with instructions not to look for the missing”.
Prostate cancer is the most common cancer in the UK, with 67,000 diagnoses annually, but is the only major cancer without a routine screening programme.
The Telegraph is campaigning for the wider introduction of targeted screening for groups at increased risk, including black men, those with a family history of prostate cancer, and carriers of other high-risk genes.
Under the plans announced in May, men with the most high-risk genetic variant and a relevant family history should receive a prostate-specific antigen (PSA) blood test every two years between the ages of 45 and 61.
However, those already known to carry BRCA2 should already be receiving regular PSA tests under existing clinical genetics guidance.
A parliamentary answer has revealed there are no plans to proactively identify additional BRCA2 carriers.
Dr Jayne Spink, the translational research director at Prostate Cancer Research, said: “The logic is impossible to follow. We’ve finally accepted that some men face a dramatically higher risk of prostate cancer, yet we’re refusing to identify most of them.
“It’s a policy that risks leaving thousands of high-risk men invisible. It’s like launching a search party with instructions not to look for the missing.”
The approach also appears at odds with consultation documents published by the UK National Screening Committee, which said Department of Health analysts were estimating the cost of identifying new BRCA carriers.
The documents stated: “DHSC analysts are undertaking an exercise to estimate the cost of identifying new BRCA variant carriers.”
![Sharon Hodgson MP](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000411953660_17875025555550_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
In response to a written parliamentary question from Peter Prinsley, a Labour MP and cancer surgeon, Sharon Hodgson, then a health minister, said in June: “The committee did not recommend proactively identifying more men with a BRCA variant, as this would constitute a separate screening programme.”
Instead, she said the best method of identifying men with a BRCA2 variant would be evaluated over time.
In response to a parliamentary question in July, Ms Hodgson said: “It is estimated that approximately 1,500 men in England will be eligible for the targeted prostate cancer screening programme.”
A Department of Health and Social Care spokesman said: “The Government is committed to improving outcomes for all men with prostate cancer, and NHS advice remains that any man with prostate cancer symptoms should get himself checked.
“We have accepted the independent expert UK National Screening Committee’s recommendation to introduce England’s first targeted prostate cancer screening programme for men with a BRCA2 gene variant and a family history of certain cancers.”
Officials added that more men would be identified through cascade testing of relatives when a BRCA variant was found, in a process already used by NHS genetics services.
The disclosure follows a separate Telegraph investigation, which found that guidance giving all men over 50 the right to request a PSA test had been withdrawn.
The right was set out repeatedly in guidance since 2002, with a recent version stating: “The PSA test is available free to men who request it.”
An accompanying flow chart for GPs was still more explicit, asking: “Does man choose to have PSA test?” If the answer was yes, the instruction was to “carry out a PSA test”.
The Department of Health has insisted the previous guidance did not amount to a right to a test, and that the final decision was always intended to lie with the GP.
However, ministers representing successive governments have repeatedly described such a right.
In 2019, Steve Brine, then a public health minister, told the Commons: “Men over 50 have the right to be given a PSA test free on the NHS once they have discussed the advantages and disadvantages with their GP.
“The PCRMP [Prostate Cancer Risk Management Programme] makes that very clear to GPs, and, having discussed the pros and cons, no one over 50 should be told ‘no’.”
The change has been condemned as an “outrageous betrayal”, with Lord Cameron, the former prime minister, who was treated for prostate cancer after taking a PSA test, describing it as a “backward step”.
summary: An upcoming NHS targeted prostate cancer screening programme in England will initially be limited to only about 1,500 men who are already known to carry a BRCA2 gene variant. Health officials currently have no plans to proactively identify the thousands of other men who unknowingly carry the variant and face an increased risk of aggressive prostate cancer. Experts and critics have condemned the limited scope of the programme for failing to find and test high-risk individuals.
key_points: Only about 1,500 men in England will receive invitations for the new targeted prostate cancer screening programme beginning next year.
The programme is restricted to men already known to carry a BRCA2 gene variant and a family history of related cancers.
An estimated 13,000 men aged 45 to 61 in England carry the BRCA2 variant, but most remain untested and unknown to officials.
Health officials stated that proactively identifying more men with a BRCA variant would constitute a separate screening programme.

title: Five food pairings that are quietly harming your health
author: Emily Craig
content:
Cheese and crackers, fish and chips, bangers and mash. Some foods just go together. However, other matches seemingly made in heaven are quietly working against you as you eat them.
“Some foods contain compounds that can reduce the absorption of certain nutrients,” explains Rob Hobson, a nutritionist and author of The Low Appetite Cookbook. These compounds, found in the likes of coffee, vegetables and fruit, makes it harder for your body to absorb vital vitamins and minerals from other foods when eaten together. When up to a third of people in the UK are deficient in key nutrients such as iron and B12, this can be problematic.
“Nutrient deficiencies almost always develop because of an overall poor diet or an underlying medical issue rather than because of one particular food combination,” notes Hobson. That said, avoiding certain pairings can bolster your vitamin and mineral intake.
Here are food combinations worth thinking twice about.
summary: Certain food combinations can negatively impact health by containing compounds that reduce the absorption of vital nutrients like iron and B12. While nutrient deficiencies are usually caused by overall poor diets or medical issues rather than a single pairing, avoiding certain combinations can help improve vitamin and mineral intake. Nutritionist Rob Hobson explains that compounds found in coffee, vegetables, and fruit can interfere with how the body absorbs nutrients from other foods eaten at the same time.
key_points: Certain food pairings can reduce the body's ability to absorb vital nutrients.
Compounds found in coffee, fruit, and vegetables can interfere with vitamin and mineral absorption.
Up to a third of people in the UK suffer from key nutrient deficiencies like iron and B12.
Nutrient deficiencies generally stem from overall poor diets or medical issues rather than isolated food combinations.
Avoiding problematic food pairings can help bolster your intake of essential vitamins and minerals.

title: This is how we do it: ‘Since having cancer, I’m more open – before I was straight, now I’m queer’
author: Naomi Larsson Piñeda
content:
Kevin, 38
 Since the all clear, my relationship with my sexuality has shifted a lot
I’ve been in recovery from drug addiction since I was 19, and I had cancer 10 years ago. So there have been points when sex has been important to me, and periods of abstaining and working on myself. Jade and I have been together for 11 years, and the sex was always good – not particularly kinky, just really intimate, nice sex.
I got ill after we’d been together less than a year and had to have one of my testicles removed, which put an immediate stop to any sex. Then I was in chemo, and sex wasn’t even on my mind – the whole period was incredibly traumatic. I’m eternally grateful that Jade stuck with me through it. Since then, my relationship with my sexuality has shifted a lot. I’ve become more vulnerable and open.
When Jade came back from a party and said a couple had asked her for a threesome, we were in a really good place. We were having sex multiple times a week, talking a lot, being open. We were actively looking for something fun, exciting and maybe a bit naughty to do. So when she asked how I felt about it, my reaction was, “I feel pretty good.”
We started going to parties and clubs together. The first time I saw Jade with a guy, I thought, “Oh, this is actually really nice.” We were instantly more attracted to each other. As soon as there was this little bit of spice, maybe even a threat, it gave us a boost. We found operating as a couple and seeing each other with other people easy. There was an instant uptick in the amount of sex we were having and how exciting it was.
I have scarring from the operation – all the lymph nodes were removed from one side of my groin, and there’s a big scar where they removed the testicle on the other side, so that was a massive blow in terms of confidence and self-image. But since exploring polyamory, I’m a far more confident person than I was before. I feel better than I ever have in my life. My relationship to my own sexuality, confidence and body is miles ahead of where it was. If you’d asked me three years ago, I would have said I was straight. I now identify as queer.
Jade, 37
 Now we date and have sex solo. It’s been a very mutual exploration
Kevin was diagnosed with cancer early on and that obviously shapes things. We had so many challenges that sex wasn’t at the forefront of my mind. But since then we found our feet, and have both been keen to explore new things.
We were monogamous for eight years, but decided to open things up three years ago. Some people do it to fix something in their relationship, but we were in a great space and wanted to share that and accelerate it with other people. A few years after Kevin got the all-clear, we were feeling exploratory and I had the opportunity to have a threesome at a party. I didn’t do it, but told Kevin I thought it would be fun, and he immediately said, “Right then, let’s do it.”
We started going to sex-positive parties and began playing together in group settings or with a third person. Now we date and have sex with other people solo. I sleep with men, women and everyone in between, and so does Kevin. It’s been a very mutual exploration.
I’d never really considered non‑monogamy before. There’s this assumed way of being that you accept, and then suddenly you discover all this richness available to you outside monogamy, and what it can bring to your relationship with your primary partner.
One of the main challenges is that we do things at different paces. Kevin is really open-hearted and forms quite strong, close relationships with people, which can create a bit of an imbalance. I’ve had to learn this balance between independence and togetherness between us.
For me, it feels great when both of our cups are full. We’re both getting meaningful, fun, exciting experiences independently of each other – and then also together.
Names have been changed
summary: Kevin and Jade, partners of 11 years, navigated Kevin's cancer diagnosis and subsequent body image challenges before deciding to open up their relationship to non-monogamy. After starting with threesomes and sex-positive parties, they both began dating and having sex with others solo. This mutual exploration ultimately boosted their confidence, increased their intimacy, and led Kevin to identify as queer.
key_points: Kevin was diagnosed with cancer less than a year into his relationship with Jade, requiring surgery and chemotherapy that halted their sex life and impacted his self-confidence.
After being monogamous for eight years and reaching a strong point in their relationship, the couple decided to open up their relationship three years ago.
They initially explored group settings and threesomes before transitioning to dating and having sex with others independently.
The journey into polyamory improved Kevin's body image and confidence, leading him to identify as queer rather than straight.
Both partners engage in solo dating with people of various genders, finding that non-monogamy has added richness to their lives and primary relationship.

title: ‘It was dark and deserted. I was drawn by the light’: Christine Rodgers’ best phone picture
author: Grace Holliday
content:
Over the last decade, Lancashire-born, London-based Christine Rodgers has trekked in Bhutan, Nepal and the Indian states and regions of Uttarakhand, Ladakh and Sikkim. “I’ve developed something of a passion for the Himalayas,” she says. “I love being in the mountains; not climbing, but walking and camping at altitude, in sight of the wonderful range of peaks.”
Rodgers used to rely on her Olympus camera to take photographs on her trips, but has since switched predominantly to using her phone. “I love the immediacy,” she notes. “I did miss having a viewfinder at first, but I now feel completely at home with the screen.”
This photograph was taken in 2024 in Melli, a town on the West Bengal-Sikkim border in northern India. It was after midnight when she arrived; her guide had stopped at the police station to collect passes for the area they would be trekking through.
“Melli was mostly dark and deserted, apart from the police station and this bank branch. I was drawn initially by the light, and the blocks of colours of paint, then by the stillness of the man at the counter. There seems to be some kind of tension in the air, caused by a customer waiting there alone at this hour of night.”
The shot is displayed in this year’s Summer Exhibition at the Royal Academy in London, one of three Rodgers took before quickly moving on. She never did find out the reason for the unease she sensed before stepping back into the night.
summary: Photographer Christine Rodgers captured a striking late-night phone image in 2024 at a bank branch in Melli, a town on the West Bengal-Sikkim border. Drawn to the light, color blocks, and a tense atmosphere involving a lone customer, she took the photo while her guide collected trekking passes. This image is now featured in London's Royal Academy Summer Exhibition.
key_points: Christine Rodgers is a Lancashire-born, London-based photographer with a passion for trekking in the Himalayas.
She has largely transitioned from using an Olympus camera to taking pictures with her phone for its immediacy.
The photograph was taken past midnight in 2024 while waiting at a police station in Melli on the West Bengal-Sikkim border.
Rodgers was drawn to the scene by the lighting, colors, and the palpable tension of a customer waiting alone at the bank.
The resulting image is one of three displayed in this year's Summer Exhibition at the Royal Academy in London.

title: When scientists disrupted dopamine in hungry rats, the animals still showed pleasure when sweet food was placed in their mouths — they just lost the drive to work for it, suggesting dopamine governs wanting more than enjoyment
author: Space Daily; Daniel Moran
content:
Strip a rat of almost all its dopamine and it will still pull a happy face at sugar.
Rats, orangutans and human newborns share a small vocabulary of facial reactions to taste. Sweetness produces rhythmic tongue protrusions and relaxed lip movements. Bitterness produces gapes and head shakes. No interview required, which makes the method unusually clean for something as slippery as pleasure.
Rats that liked sugar and did nothing about it
Kent Berridge and Terry Robinson, in a University of Michigan laboratory, used a neurotoxin to destroy up to 99 per cent of the dopamine in the nucleus accumbens and neostriatum of rats. In a long review published in Brain Research Reviews, they reported that the animals’ facial reactions to sucrose came through the procedure intact. Their willingness to seek it out collapsed. Left alone with food in the cage, they barely touched it.
Two systems, apparently, sharing one word.
Mice that cannot make dopamine at all
Claire Cannon and Richard Palmiter took a blunter approach at the University of Washington, breeding mice genetically incapable of synthesising dopamine. Their paper in the Journal of Neuroscience, titled Reward without Dopamine, put the animals in front of a computerised lickometer and watched what they chose. They chose sucrose over water, and saccharin too, a sweetener with no calories at all, which rules out a simple energy-seeking explanation. Even juveniles that had never once eaten with their dopamine system switched on already showed the same preference.
What went missing was the fetching. The mice initiated drinking bouts less often and took fewer licks overall than normal mice. Without a daily dose of L-dopa, they will starve next to a full dish.
Turning the dial the other way
Push synaptic dopamine up instead of wiping it out, and the same split shows up in reverse. Susana Peciña and colleagues bred mutant mice that keep only a tenth of the normal dopamine transporter, leaving them swimming in roughly 70 per cent more synaptic dopamine than usual. Writing in the same journal, the team clocked these mice reaching a sweet reward faster and with far less fumbling than ordinary mice managed. Their facial liking reactions to sucrose sat at baseline.
A test built around effort
Put a hungry rat in a cage with two ways to eat: a lever that pays out sugar pellets, or a bowl of plain chow sitting there for free. John Salamone and Mercè Correa built decades of research around exactly this choice. Give the rat a low dose of the dopamine blocker haloperidol and lever pressing collapses while chow intake holds steady, an effect Patrick Randall and colleagues documented in a progressive ratio study in PLoS One.
The animal still wants dinner. It has simply stopped being willing to pay for it.
Salamone and Correa’s Neuron paper puts the conclusion bluntly: calling these cells reward neurons is an overgeneralisation. On their reading, accumbens dopamine handles behavioural activation, exertion of effort, approach and sustained engagement. Appetite itself lives somewhere else.
Where the pleasure actually lives
That somewhere else turned out to be tiny. Berridge later mapped it with Morten Kringelbach, describing hedonic hotspots in Pleasure systems in the brain, patches roughly a cubic millimetre across in the accumbens shell and at the back of the ventral pallidum. Opioid or orexin stimulation there can more than double a rat’s liking reactions to sweetness. Dopamine stimulation in the very same tissue lifts the urge to eat and leaves the liking flat.
Wanting, on this account, runs on large and robust machinery. Liking depends on something small enough to knock over by accident.
How settled is any of this
Some caution belongs here. This is one research programme, and a contested one. Other labs treat dopamine less as a reward signal and more as a teaching mechanism, a prediction error that quietly updates expectations. Others cast it instead as a controller of movement vigour. Robinson and Berridge published a defence of their incentive sensitisation theory in the Annual Review of Psychology, three decades after proposing it, which tells you how live the argument still is.
The dissociation has been robust enough to reshape how addiction gets described. Craving that outlasts enjoyment stops looking mysterious once the two run on separate circuitry, and a drug that sensitises one system has no obligation to touch the other. People who report that a substance stopped being fun years ago, and who chase it anyway, are describing something a rat can demonstrate on camera.
Which offers a cold sort of comfort to anyone who has scrolled for an hour and enjoyed roughly none of it. Pull and payoff were never welded together in the first place.
summary: Scientific studies on rats and mice with depleted or enhanced dopamine reveal that the neurotransmitter governs the drive to work for food rather than the pleasure of tasting it. While dopamine-depleted animals still display normal facial reactions of enjoyment to sweet tastes, they lose the motivation to seek out or expend effort for food. Conversely, boosting dopamine increases the speed and effort of reaching a reward without altering the baseline facial reactions of liking it. These findings demonstrate a distinct separation between "wanting" and "liking" in the brain, helping explain phenomena like addiction where craving persists long after enjoyment has faded.
key_points: Rats and mice with severely depleted or absent dopamine still show normal facial expressions of pleasure when given sweet food.
Despite enjoying the taste, dopamine-depleted rodents lose the motivation to work for food and will starve near a full dish if effort is required.
Elevating synaptic dopamine increases the speed and effort used to reach a reward without changing the baseline pleasure reaction.
Brain mapping identifies tiny "hedonic hotspots" driven by opioids and orexin that control pleasure, while dopamine handles the urge and effort to eat.
This neurological separation of wanting and liking reshapes how addiction and compulsive behaviors are understood, as craving can vastly outlast enjoyment.

title: Semaglutide slimming jab study aims to help alcohol dependency
author: Rob Sissons
content:
![A close-up of an anonymous man holding a tumbler filled with dark alcohol and ice](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1280/cpsprodpb/92ee/live/2b7d2240-bdeb-11ef-a2ca-e99d0c9a24e3.jpg)
If successful, the study could lead to a new treatment for alcohol-related liver disease and obesity
- Published
A Â£2.7m clinical trial will investigate if a weight-loss jab can help patients living with alcohol dependency and obesity, which the NHS said were two of the biggest causes of liver disease.
The four-year study will examine the impact of the weight-loss drug semaglutide, which is also known as Wegovy.
Teams in Nottingham and Plymouth are leading the research and, from next month, plan to recruit about 270 NHS patients who are both dependent on alcohol and obese from across the UK.
The aim is to develop a new treatment for alcohol-related liver disease and obesity.
Alcohol misuse is a leading cause of preventable death, and costs the NHS an estimated Â£5bn a year.
![An image of a Wegovy weight loss drug injector pen](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/7ccc/live/a9f280b0-9d51-11f1-aac2-870643eea2ac.jpg)
Half of the patients involved in the trial will be given weekly injections of semaglutide, also known as Wegovy
Researchers at the National Institute for Health and Care Research's Biomedical Research Centre in Nottingham are working with the University of Plymouth to jointly lead the study.
Half of the 268 recruits will be given weekly injections of semaglutide, while the other half will receive a placebo over 36 weeks.
The launch of this latest study follows a growing body of research into the link between weight-loss drugs and alcohol consumption.
Drugs such as Wegovy and Ozempic contain semaglutide, while Mounjaro contains tirzepatide.
These medicines mimic the naturally occurring hormone GLP-1, helping to suppress appetite and keep people feeling fuller for longer.
Some users of weight-loss drugs have reported it is changing their relationship with alcohol and reducing cravings, and this is the latest study to examine that link in more detail.
![Professor Guru Aithal stood outside Nottingham's Queen's Medical Centre wearing a blue shirt](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1536/cpsprodpb/14d3/live/c66aba50-9d6f-11f1-bdcc-8926c4a74c43.jpg)
Prof Guru Aithal hopes the study will demonstrate the "potential for a new NHS treatment"
Prof Guru Aithal, deputy director of the centre, said the main aim of the investigation was to determine if the drug could reduce patients' alcohol intake while also helping them lose weight and improve their liver health and quality of life.
To get on the study, NHS patients have to have a body mass index of least 30, have an alcohol use disorder,, external and evidence of scarring of the liver or cirrhosis.
Harmful drinking is the leading cause of liver disease in the UK, and Aithal said the UK "has experienced higher rates of deaths from alcohol-related liver disease compared to other European countries over the past four decades".
"The combination of alcohol and obesity act together to speed up liver damage and death in patients, and both these conditions are difficult to treat with current medicines and counselling," he added.
"I hope that we can successfully evidence the impact of weight-loss drugs to curb alcohol intake and demonstrate the cost effectiveness and potential for a new NHS treatment."
Prof Ashwin Dhanda, a liver medicine specialist at the University of Plymouth, said: "We see patients who are dependent on alcohol and are obese every day, but there is currently no treatment that targets obesity and alcohol use at the same time."
He added: "We need to seize this opportunity."
Listen to BBC Radio Nottingham on Sounds and follow BBC Nottingham on Facebook, external, on X, external, or on Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to eastmidsnews@bbc.co.uk, external or via WhatsApp, external on 0808 100 2210.
- ![A group of women are sat in a bar - one is being offered a glass of wine and she is holding up her hand to say "no"](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/3dba/live/f6aa7180-91a6-11f1-a7ab-8b30adf0800a.jpg)
- ![A woman wearing a white t-shirt holds a white injectable medicine pen in front of her stomach](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/8acf/live/3d322ee0-8c86-11ef-8537-35d6ce5671fe.jpg)
  - Published13 January 2025
 ![Ray, a 62-year-old man with closely cropped hair, smiling slightly as he looks towards the camera during an interview at his home.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/960/cpsprodpb/4c93/live/d8a57de0-d183-11ef-87df-d575b9a434a4.jpg)
summary: A new £2.7m clinical trial will investigate whether the weight-loss drug semaglutide can help patients suffering from both alcohol dependency and obesity. Led by teams in Nottingham and Plymouth, the four-year study will recruit about 270 NHS patients to determine if the drug reduces alcohol intake while improving liver health and weight. Researchers hope the findings will establish a new, effective NHS treatment for conditions that are major causes of liver disease and preventable death.
key_points: A £2.7m four-year clinical trial is investigating if the weight-loss drug semaglutide (Wegovy) can treat alcohol dependency and obesity.
The study aims to recruit approximately 270 NHS patients across the UK who have a BMI of at least 30, an alcohol use disorder, and evidence of liver scarring or cirrhosis.
Half of the participants will receive weekly injections of semaglutide and the other half will receive a placebo over a 36-week period.
Researchers hope the trial will demonstrate that weight-loss drugs can curb alcohol intake, improve liver health, and provide a cost-effective new NHS treatment.

title: The enjoyable exercise better than walking for lifelong fitness
author: Harry Bullmore
content:
“When you settle into a rhythm, it feels like flying,” INWA Nordic walking instructor Katie Atkins tells me. “Even when you see people out walking nowadays, they’re on their phones. But Nordic walking is a technology detox. You can’t hold a phone because you have a pole in each hand. For the time you’re walking, you have the chance to just be; to chat and to enjoy what’s around you.”
Millions of people across Europe use Nordic walking to keep themselves in shape. The UK has been slower to adopt the activity, particularly among younger people, but Nordic4 founder Atkins says we’re missing out on benefits both above and below the neck.
This low-impact pastime puts upwards of 80 per cent of your muscles to work – far more than regular walking. Research suggests it also burns considerably more calories, holds greater heart health perks, does a better job of boosting fitness and offers greater protection against many chronic diseases than a standard stroll.
“I played a lot of tennis before, and I found the right side of my body was much stronger and more coordinated than the left side,” Atkins adds. “The thing I’ve really noticed in the last 16 years of Nordic walking is it’s really good for balancing the body up.”
A healthier, fitter and more balanced body is an attractive prospect. So is the idea you can build one with an accessible, social and enjoyable form of exercise.
If this pitch has sold you on the idea of Nordic walking, here’s how to get started.
How to start Nordic walking
Nordic walking is more than just walking with poles, as the video above explains. There needs to be a considerable focus on technique when you first start.
The first step is to practice walking with an upright posture and a natural arm swing. Next, you need a set of walking poles with straps.
“The straps are really important,” Atkins says. “They enable you to propel yourself forward, then extend your arm and release your grip, before catching the pole again as your arm swings forward. People talk about sculpted ‘Nordic arms’ because you’re working your triceps with every step.”
One common beginner mistake is holding the poles upright. Instead, they should remain at roughly a 45-degree angle, allowing you to push the ground away and propel yourself forward each time yours arms swing backwards.
“You also want to be looking ahead, strike the ground with your heel first and have good postural alignment with a slight forward lean from the ankles – like you get in cross country skiing,” Atkins adds. “That activates your glutes, then your arms and core are engaged as you push through the pole, and your legs are working too.
“Used correctly, the poles enhance your walk. As you push through them, you actually feel the load on your knees and hips lighten. It’s lower impact than activities like running.”
For this reason, she says it is suitable for everyone from Olympic athletes seeking improved performance to those over 60 or looking to rehab an injury.
You can follow the advice above to get a good grounding in Nordic walking. However, much of the appeal and many of the perks come from doing it as a group. Instructor-led sessions are also the best way to fine-tune your technique, Atkins says, with many groups offering taster sessions.
You can find your nearest INWA (International Nordic Walking Federation) certified group on the British Nordic Walking interactive map.
Read more: How just 20 minutes of walking a day can transform your health
![Nordic walking can improve health and fitness in people of all ages and ability levels, instructor Katie Atkins says](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/21/10/36/Nordic-walking-INWA-images.jpeg)
A sample Nordic walking session for beginners
Neil Yoxall, an experienced hiker and sales manager for outdoor equipment specialists Silva, suggests the session below for anyone looking to get a feel for Nordic walking.
- Start with a five-minute warm-up walk at a relaxed pace, don’t worry too much about speed.
- Spend 15-20 minutes Nordic walking at a pace comfortable to you, focusing on technique and rhythm.
- Every five minutes, spend 30 seconds exaggerating the push through the poles to feel the extra upper-body engagement.
- Finish with a five-minute cool-down walk and some gentle mobility stretches using the poles.
“When you first try, it's more important to build confidence in the movement than to chase distance or intensity,” he explains. “Once your technique feels natural, you can gradually increase either the duration, pace or the types of terrain you're covering.”
Read more: Scientists share six easy ways to increase the health benefits of your daily walk
![Nordic walking boosts physical and mental health while providing a social hit](https://static.independent.co.uk/2025/11/12/13/43/New-research-from-the-University-of-Sydney-suggests-more-intense-exercise-can-deliver-several-health.jpeg)
The benefits
“The poles effectively turn walking into a coordinated whole-body movement,” says Yoxall. “Every time you plant a pole and push backwards, you're generating force through the upper body while maintaining a natural walking gait. This extra muscular involvement increases the overall work your body is doing and encourages an upright posture.
“At the same time, some of the impact and effort that would normally be absorbed solely by the lower body is distributed through the arms and shoulders.”
The lower impact nature of Nordic walking is one of its major pull factors. This is partly because there is a well-worn path for amateur athletes.
Team sports tend to dominate their teens and twenties, solo endurance endeavours such as running take over in their thirties, then joint pain sees them switch to cycling and swimming in their 40s and beyond. With busy lives and injuries, participation often tails off over time.
But, Atkins argues, Nordic walking is an activity that can serve you through every season of life.
“When you go to mainland Europe, people very much see Nordic walking as a sport – you see it everywhere and it’s part of their way of life,” she says. “It’s regarded as an activity that Olympic athletes can use to train. They’re a bit ahead of the game compared to where we are in the UK. Here, it’s often seen as an activity for older people and middle-aged women, but that is changing now, which is exciting to see.
“You can Nordic walk from childhood right up to old age, building physical literacy for life.”
Read more: The easiest way to strengthen your entire body, according to this expert coach
![The use of poles can take stress away from the hip, knee and ankle joints, delivering a lower impact form of cardiovascular exercise than running](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/07/03/11/20/A-woman-Nordic-walking-in-the-woods.jpeg)
Nordic walking also takes place outside, delivering the many well-documented mental and physical health benefits that come with getting out of the house and into nature. And it puts you in a group setting.
“Nordic walking is an opportunity to connect with other people, and with nature,” says Atkins. “There’s nothing like seeing the seasons change and really noticing everything around you. It also gives you the opportunity to explore different terrain, which you might not feel comfortable doing on your own.”
There is a learning element involved too, with adopting new skills being one of the best things you can do to maintain a healthy brain, according to Harvard Health. Atkins likens an introduction to Nordic walking to learning to drive.
“When you start, you have to think about checking your mirrors, using your indicators and performing certain manoeuvres. Then, with practice, it all goes into muscle memory.”
Learning to coordinate her body in this way helped Atkins strengthen her body and swerve injuries, despite having hypermobility.
“The poles keep me aligned, allowing my muscles and joints to become stronger,” she says. “Everything is being used in the way it should be used, rather than being very loose. I think, without Nordic walking, I would otherwise have had problems in my joints.”
![People competing in a Nordic walking race](<https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/21/10/15/Nordic-walking-INWA-images-(1).jpeg>)
The best poles to buy
The most important thing when finding the best walking poles is to find a set built specifically for Nordic walking, with a strap attached to the handle, Atkins says. She favours Leki poles, while brands such as Silva, Exel and Gabel also offer good options from around £50. A price point of £80-£90 often offers the best balance between quality and value, Atkins adds.
Beyond this, there is a great deal of personal preference at play, as well as several individual factors to consider.
“It’s all related to your height and proportions,” Atkins explains. “You might have someone who is 5ft 4in, so you assume they need a specific pole height, but they could have a very short upper body and very long legs. That’s why I’d recommend going to a retailer who can advise you properly.”
A strong, lightweight pole is preferable, as this will deliver durability and a more enjoyable walking experience. A higher carbon content tends to deliver on both fronts, Atkins says. If you plan to use your poles while travelling, a pair that can collapse into segments and be packed away can also be handy.
Read more: Do this for three months and transform your fitness for years
![Members of a Nordic walking class using the poles to stretch and improve mobility (International Nordic Walking Federation)](<https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/21/10/28/Nordic-walking-INWA-images-(2).jpeg>)
Other ways to strengthen your body through Nordic walking
There are few areas of the body that aren’t active while Nordic walking. But there are extra exercises you can do with the poles to build further strength, mobility and balance.
These range from standard exercises like overhead presses, pole-supported lunges and squats – planting a pole in the ground to hold on to for support – to more novel movements.
“There’s one exercise that I call crackers,” says Atkins. “You hold the pole out in front of you with your arms parallel to the ground and your hands shoulder-width apart. Then the hands stay still, but you try to pull the pole apart like a cracker for five to 20 seconds, strengthening the upper body.
“Or you can do the reverse cracker, holding the pole in the same way but trying to squeeze your hands together, filling in other parts of the upper body. It feels great.”
“Walking poles can double as a simple fitness tool,” adds Yoxall. “Before or after a walk, you can use them for mobility exercises such as torso rotations, chest-opening stretches and shoulder mobility drills. They can also be incorporated into balance exercises, supported squats, lunges and calf stretches.”
Read more: You don’t need to lift weights for strength training – these exercises count too
summary: Nordic walking is an accessible, low-impact exercise that engages upwards of 80 percent of the body's muscles and burns more calories than standard walking. The activity utilizes specialized poles with straps, turning a regular walk into a coordinated, full-body movement that reduces strain on the hips, knees, and ankles. Suitable for all fitness levels from children to older adults, it provides both physical and mental health benefits while serving as a social and outdoor activity.
key_points: Nordic walking engages over 80 percent of muscles and burns more calories than regular walking.
Proper technique requires specific poles with straps, an upright posture, and a 45-degree pole angle to propel the body forward.
The use of poles distributes impact away from the lower body, lightening the load on knees and hips.
Group and instructor-led sessions help beginners fine-tune their technique while offering social and mental health benefits.

title: 7 surprising signs that show you're pretty healthy, actually
author: Jessica Lindsay
content:
![](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/GettyImages-1989500628-17e4.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
From heart rate to sleep score, it’s de rigueur nowadays to be constantly monitoring your health through smart tech.
While useful for some, for others it becomes more anxiety-inducing than galvanising — which can itself have counterproductive physical consequences.
By shifting your focus to what’s wrong, they can also mean you don’t recognise when things are going well.
But if you take a step back and listen to your body’s signals, from how you feel to what you can do, you may see that you’re not doing too bad after all.
As Dr Donald Grant, GP and senior clinical advisor at The Independent Pharmacy highlights, there’s no single ‘pass or fail test for how healthy you are,’ and regular medical checkups are important for everyone.
That said, there are certain indicators that can provide a reassuring reminder you’re on the right track (provided you’re able-bodied and don’t have underlying conditions which impact your mobility or bodily functions).
After TikTok creator Josh Fraser Young shared his own now-viral list of health signals, Metro asked medical professionals which ones they agree with, and what they also recommend looking out for.
Ready to reframe your outlook?
You can put your socks on standing up
This may sound like a basic task to some, but single leg balance is one of the strongest predictors of longevity.
Ask Metro
Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.
In fact, as Josh explains, a 2022 study found older people who couldn’t stand on one leg for 10 seconds had an 84% higher risk of dying within 10 years.
Dr Grant calls this ‘a genuinely useful marker rather than just a party trick,’ adding: ‘Balance relies on a combination of muscle strength, joint stability, and the nervous system, all working together. That combination tends to decline gradually with age or inactivity before people notice it in daily life.’
![](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/GettyImages-1444073060-3499.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
But Kelly Fisher, health and wellbeing Nurse at Benenden Health also notes that not being able to do this doesn’t mean you are unhealthy.
‘There could be lots of reasons stopping you such as muscle tightness or joint stiffness, and many of the people in the study mentioned also had other health conditions such as obesity and heart disease,’ she tells Metro.
If you’re struggling, she advises gentle stretching exercises like yoga to help build flexibility, as well as working on your balance by incorporating single leg balances into your daily routine.
She adds: ‘Try practicing for 30 seconds on each leg while you brush your teeth or waiting for the kettle to boil.’
You can get up from the floor without using your hands
‘Try it, without using your hands, knees, or furniture,’ says Josh in his video. ‘It requires strength, balance, mobility, coordination, and power all at once. Studies show that people who can do this tend to live longer than those who can’t.’
Kelly agrees, explaining: ‘This movement can be a really great indicator of your aerobic fitness, muscle and core strength, stability, flexibility and balance which are all key thing we need to age healthily and reduce the risk of injuries from falls.’
Can you get up from the floor without using your hands?
- 
						Yep, it's easy!
- 
						I struggle, but manage it eventually.
- 
						No chance.
As with the sock exercise though, Dr Grant says: ‘Finding this harder than it used to be is common as people become less active, and on its own isn’t a cause for alarm.
‘If it’s become consistently difficult, or is accompanied by joint pain or stiffness, it’s worth having checked, since it can sometimes point to reduced muscle mass or an underlying joint issue.’
You have a firm grip
According to Dr Grant, ‘grip strength is one of the more reliable indicators on [Josh’s list].’
‘It reflects overall muscle strength and neurological function, and research has linked weaker grip strength to a higher risk of frailty and even cognitive decline in later life, which is more than can be said for most quick physical tests,’ he continues.
Once again, however, Kelly highlights that while it ‘may give a useful indication of overall health,’ it’s ‘important that it’s not used as a standalone value and that individual circumstances are also considered.’
![](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/GettyImages-1495755084-48dc.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
You get hungry at regular times
‘Consistent hunger signals mean your metabolism and hunger hormones are well regulated,’ says Josh.
And Dr Grant echoes this, explaining that it ‘can reflect settled blood sugar and eating patterns.’
‘It is still useful to pay attention to those hungry feelings,’ caveats Kelly. ‘Sometimes they can appear when we are bored or stressed, sometimes referred as emotional eating, or they may become supressed if you have a high caffeine intake.’
You can hold a deep, flat-footed squat
We’re not talking about a typical gym squat here; rather a resting squat you hold without your heels lifting.
‘Being able to hold a flat-footed squat does say something about hip and ankle mobility, but is shaped by habit and lifestyle as much as underlying health,’ explains Dr Grant.
Kelly continues: ‘Tightness in your ankles and hips can make this a difficult manoeuvre along with spending long periods of the day sitting down.
‘Practicing deep squats can help with these issues, and a great way is to do the squat with your legs either side of a sturdy doorframe. The doorframe can help you to maintain your balance while your build up to being able to do the movement unsupported.’
![](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/GettyImages-1332112356-edd1.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
You can climb a few flights of stairs without getting breathless
Although not included on Josh’s list, Dr Grant says being able to climb a few flights of stairs without becoming breathless (at least not to the point you’re seriously struggling) can ‘prove useful in measuring health.’
The four-flight stair climb test is actually recommended by the European Society of Cardiology, to help determine overall heart health alongside risk of cardiac conditions.
In studies, those who were able to climb four flights (about 60 steps) at a brisk, steady pace with no stopping and minimal breathlessness in less than 90 seconds were deemed to be at lower risk.
On the contrary, those who needed to stop or experienced significant shortness of breath or chest pain had a higher chance of developing coronary artery disease — so if that’s the case for you, it could be time to visit your doctor.
You wake up feeling rested
Although Josh highlights waking up before your alarm as a marker of tip-top health, Kelly says it’s a little more nuanced than this.
In her view, quality of rest is a better indicator, as ‘if you feel groggy when you wake up this can be a sign that you have had a poor quality sleep.’
Numerous studies have linked linked the long-term lack of quality rest to a range of issues, from heart disease and type 2 diabetes to cognitive decline and mental health disorders.

	![Young woman in bed with her arms by her head](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_307896638-cbfc.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0px%2C0px%2C2500px%2C1406px&resize=646%2C363)
- My childhood babysitter and I are having sex – my parents will be so mad if they find out
- Dirty hotel sex made up for this big disappointment after 10 years of marriage
- Iconic '90s chocolate bar with controversial past makes its return to Asda's shelves
Basically, it’s not just about how many hours of shut-eye you get, but that it’s uninterrupted and leaves you feeling refreshed in the morning.
Keep in mind, these aren’t hard and fast rules; they’re merely designed to help you take a broader, more positive look at your health rather than worrying about every little fluctuation.
And even if you tick all these boxes, you should still be mindful of other potential symptoms.

‘It can be easy to ignore those niggling signals, but these are messages our body is using to tell us something is wrong,’ adds Kelly. ‘Make sure during those busier times you spend a few minutes each day checking in with yourself so the messages don’t go unanswered.’
