‘We were told she was constipated at the GP,’ Anna explains. ‘For three weeks I had to force-feed her laxatives which was horrendous.’
The young mum says Florence was crying in pain and was unable to sleep on her own because she was in agony. Anna had to cradle her upright at night to help her get some rest.
‘When her stomach hadn’t gone down, doctors gave her more laxatives, but it was getting bigger,’ she says. ‘She wasn’t right and the laxatives weren’t helping so we had to keep pushing the doctors.’
But despite the parents’ growing concerns, doctors dismissed them. ‘On one occasion a GP said she’s fine and “let’s address the elephant in the room, we don’t think it’s cancer”,’ she adds.
They went to the doctor again for a final time, accompanied by Anna’s mother, who pushed for a blood test.
![Florence Wilde, in hospital with her father Dom. // A toddler whose belly ballooned was diagnosed with a 2kg tumour after doctors repeatedly told her parents she was constipated. Florence Wilde, two, was diagnosed with neuroblastoma - a rare cancer of the cell - in November 2024. Her parents Anna Chattaway and Dom Wilde, both 32, first noticed something was wrong when Florence became repeatedly rundown. The toddler's tummy began to swell so the pair rushed her to Three Villages GP in Stourbridge but doctors ruled out the symptoms as constipation, prescribing the tot laxatives. Photo released 21/08/2026](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308994199-ad10-e1787394604609.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=600) 
‘Her bloods were heightened and they referred us to the PAU (paediatric assessment unit) immediately,’ she says. ‘We had another doctor who felt her stomach. As soon as he felt her tummy he said he didn’t think it was poo, there were lumps and bumps.’
Anna says Florence was reassured her symptoms were constipation on at least six occasions in the three weeks before her diagnosis.
‘When the tumour was discovered it was 30cm, which was heart-breaking,’ she recalls. ‘She’s only small so that took up quite a lot of her.’
Florence underwent surgery at Birmingham Children’s Hospital on November 26, 2024 and started emergency chemotherapy the very next day.
Anna adds: ‘She had three months of induction chemotherapy to try and shrink the tumour. They thought the disease was in one place, in her stomach, they assumed it was localised.’
Sadly, further scans in January 2025 revealed Florence had metastatic, or stage 4 cancer, which happens when cells break away from the main tumour. In this case the disease spread to her spine.
![Anna Chattaway and Dom Wilde, with their daughter Florence. // A toddler whose belly ballooned was diagnosed with a 2kg tumour after doctors repeatedly told her parents she was constipated. Florence Wilde, two, was diagnosed with neuroblastoma - a rare cancer of the cell - in November 2024. Her parents Anna Chattaway and Dom Wilde, both 32, first noticed something was wrong when Florence became repeatedly rundown. The toddler's tummy began to swell so the pair rushed her to Three Villages GP in Stourbridge but doctors ruled out the symptoms as constipation, prescribing the tot laxatives. Photo released 21/08/2026](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308994185-6559-e1787394694436.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=600) 
‘We look back now, how did we think she was constipated because her stomach was massive?’ Anna says.
‘It grew rapidly in a few weeks, that’s why we have so much anger because if someone would have seen her the first time we went to the GP we could’ve caught this sooner.’
She had up to 95% of the tumour removed from her spine in March 2025, before beginning her first rounds of high-dose chemo just three weeks later.
Florence began five cycles of immunotherapy in October that year, before her parents were eventually told the tumour had stopped progressing in April 2026.
‘All throughout we were told she was doing great,’ Anna says. ‘Every admission she was full of life throughout it, she was just incredible.
‘We’ve met families along the way who have been pushed back from GP’s and doctors more than what Florence’s has.
‘For us, I do think if she was diagnosed sooner it might have not been that large. We sat in that headspace for many months and it was horrifying. There was a lot of anger there.’
The family are now fundraising £100,000 to pay for anti-relapse treatment (DMFO) no longer offered by the NHS, after the treatment was withdrawn by the manufacturer from standard UK access routes, forcing people to pay for it out of their own pocket.
![Anna Chattaway and Dom Wilde, with their daughter Florence. // A toddler whose belly ballooned was diagnosed with a 2kg tumour after doctors repeatedly told her parents she was constipated. Her parents Anna Chattaway and Dom Wilde, both 32, first noticed something was wrong when Florence became repeatedly rundown. The toddler's tummy began to swell so the pair rushed her to Three Villages GP in Stourbridge but doctors ruled out the symptoms as constipation, prescribing the tot laxatives. Photo released 21/08/2026](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308994181-f341-e1787394768476.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=600) 
‘Florence has finished the gold standard NHS treatment, after that you can either watch and wait to see if the cancer comes back, or other families chose to do a relapse prevention treatment, but they aren’t NHS protocol,’ Anna says.

Despite all she’s faced, Florence has beaten the 50% survival odds of the childhood cancer and her parents are proud.
‘She’s been doing incredibly, she’s such a happy little girl. Life is good at home,’ Anna says.

title: Seven simple ways to maintain muscle strength later in life
author: Camilla Foster
content:
As we age, many people notice small changes that make them feel a little weaker or slower.
Lucy Macdonald, a physiotherapist based in Surrey at Restart Physio, says many often don’t realise the cause is sarcopenia.
Here’s exactly what sarcopenia is and tips on how to stay strong later in life.
What is sarcopenia?
“Age-related sarcopenia is the process by which muscles get weaker as you get older,” explains Macdonald.
This condition is caused by a combination of factors, including the natural ageing process, physical inactivity and changes to hormonal levels.
“There are some factors, like hormonal changes, that people can’t do anything about. For example, decreasing levels of testosterone in men and women as they get older can be a factor,” says Macdonald. “However, we are in control of our activity levels.
![Sarcopenia is caused by a combination of factors](https://static.the-independent.com/2025/12/03/14/03092516-6ac8fa45-521a-4cbc-8504-aaa94cfbbdcf.jpg)
“A lot of people will reduce their activity levels, in part just because of general lifestyle but also sometimes because of fear of injury, and actually these things can significantly contribute to muscle wasting as well.”
She highlights that she usually sees sarcopenia in patients who are in two particular phases of life.
“The first one would be people in their late 40s because around that age, people’s lives tend to be very busy,” says Macdonald. “They’ve got busy careers and often have caring responsibilities for kids and older relatives. So, in terms of the amount of time they have to stay active, that’s quite a sort of crunch point.
“Sarcopenia is also very prevalent in the early 60s age range. At this age, people are thinking of retiring which is another turning point as some people will have a really active retirement and some will do considerably less.”
What are some symptoms that might suggest you have sarcopenia?
“Finding it difficult to get out of a chair or to go up and down stairs easily are two key indicators,” says Macdonald. “If you start to notice that you’re struggling a bit to get that power to do these things without using your upper body, I would seek professional advice about this.”
How can sarcopenia impact your daily life?
“Day-to-day things like carrying your shopping or playing with the grandkids might become difficult,” says Macdonald. “So many things involve physical activity, and if you haven’t got the muscle strength to do it you’re going to start to enjoy these activities less.
![Sarcopenia is also very prevalent in the early 60s age range](https://static.the-independent.com/2025/12/03/14/03093242-2cdc0e04-f0e5-45a0-b113-42581d218f53.jpg)
“It could also become painful to do things. Sarcopenia is considered to be a significant contributing factor to joint pain which can really affect people’s quality of life.”
Can you slow down the progression of sarcopenia or prevent it?
“The best thing to do to slow down the progression of sarcopenia or to prevent it is strength work,” says Macdonald. “A physio can give you specific exercises to strengthen your muscles in relation to the things that you want to be able to achieve.
“For example, if you wanted to be able to take your grandchildren to the park, then a physio can help you strengthen the muscles that are involved in that.”
What are your top tips for building and maintaining muscle later in life?
Try sit and stand exercises
“When you’ve just got out of bed in the morning, try sitting on the edge of your bed and standing up and sitting down again in a controlled way, and repeat that 30 times,” says Macdonald. “Sit to stand is basically a squat and you can progress by adding a bit of weight to this exercise or try doing it on a lower surface, such as a sofa.”
Wall press-ups
“Lean as much of your body weight as you can against your hands on a wall, and then just gently bend and straighten your elbows,” recommends Macdonald.
Introduce weights under the guidance of a professional
“Slowly introduce some lifting exercises under the guidance of either a physio or a personal trainer,” recommends Macdonald. “They will help you learn a bit more about your own body and how important strength is, and will also provide some encouragement.”
Increase the weight gradually
“If you suddenly launch into doing weights, you will probably get injured,” warns Macdonald. “By overloading them, you’ll get tears in the muscle, which can be very painful and you’ll end up weaker, rather than stronger. So, you want to start low and increase the weight gradually.”
Join a group
“There are lots of groups out there where you can go and do resistance training and use weights in a group setting,” says Macdonald. “The advantage of doing exercise in a group is that you’re more likely to stick to it.”
Don’t be afraid
“Try not to let fear get in the way of getting strong,” advises Macdonald. “Although fear of injury is very normal, fear often ends up increasing the likelihood of getting injured because if you don’t use it, you lose it.”
Remember that losing strength isn’t inevitable
“Just because it’s harder to be strong as we get older doesn’t mean that it’s not possible,” says Macdonald. “I’ve seen some incredibly strong older people, so there’s full potential to be strong later in life. You have control over it, so getting weaker and weaker as you age is not an inevitable thing.”
summary: Age-related sarcopenia is a condition where muscles get weaker due to factors like the natural aging process, hormonal changes, and physical inactivity. Physiotherapist Lucy Macdonald notes that it is often prevalent in people during their late 40s and early 60s when lifestyles change. However, individuals can manage or prevent muscle wasting by staying active, performing strength exercises, and gradually introducing weights under professional guidance.
key_points: Sarcopenia is caused by a combination of aging, hormonal shifts, and reduced physical activity.
Common indicators include struggling to rise from a chair or walk up and down stairs easily.
Strength work, such as sit-and-stand exercises and wall press-ups, can slow or prevent muscle loss.
Lifting weights should be introduced and increased gradually under professional supervision to avoid injury.
Maintaining strength later in life is controllable and not an inevitable consequence of aging.

title: Heartbroken woman tells boyfriend 'leave me' after being diagnosed with aggressive cancer - AOL
author: Liam McInerney
content:
![Mirror UK](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/logos/light/mirror-uk.png?v=1784567839)
![Lydia Whelan](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/08/21/b9891b21-2d0c-3504-a3b2-64c0b4616c56/8cb5539f-3d7b-4cf9-bc47-02edbc5b22ea.jpg)
A woman revealed the heartbreaking conversations she had with her loved ones after being diagnosed with breast cancer at the age of just 32 — including telling her boyfriend to leave her.
Lydia Whelan and her long-term partner Colm had just been given the green light on a house sale agreement when their lives took an unexpected turn two years ago.
Just one week before the sale was agreed, Lydia, who is from County Kildare, Ireland, was visiting her doctor after spotting a change in her breast.
And on July 30, 2024, Colm was by Lydia’s side at St James’s Hospital in Dublin when a doctor confirmed she had cancer. It was later confirmed to be aggressive and stage two.
In an emotional interview with Dublin Dialogues, Lydia remembered: “I just erupted and my partner erupted and I was like, ‘I knew it.’
![Lydia Whelan](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/08/21/b9891b21-2d0c-3504-a3b2-64c0b4616c56/29f6d674-5a00-4ce9-97c9-6d124fe35da4.jpg)
“Then very quickly I was like, ‘How am I going to tell my mother?’ It was all like a lot of emotions and feelings kind of came at once and I found myself sitting there… myself and my partner after going ‘sale agreed’ on our home in the middle of all this.
“So that was very daunting.”
Due to her diagnosis, Lydia, a support worker for adults with intellectual disabilities, could not get approval for mortgage protection, and there was a fear that she could lose the house.
And being remarkably honest, she said: “I have said it before to a lot of people, I was more upset about the potential of losing my house than I was of being told I had cancer because I was looking at the future, myself and my partner for 10 years together at that point, this was the next stage for us.”
She added: “I was like, ‘I don’t know how I’m going to cope.’ If we lose our house, I was telling him to leave me. I was like, ‘I’m holding you back.’
![Lydia and Colm](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/08/21/b9891b21-2d0c-3504-a3b2-64c0b4616c56/17a0df03-3c30-4daa-ae09-33c4f9da88ee.jpg)
“It’s conversations that you don’t expect to have at the age of 32.”
And in another heartbreaking conversation, this time with her parents, she revealed: “I remember going home to my mum and dad and I was still living at home at this point and I just burst out crying. I was like, ‘I don’t want to lose my hair.’”
Thankfully, Lydia’s partner, family and friends offered nothing but love and support, and she said she would not have gotten through her treatment without them.
Lydia is now a cancer survivor after several brutal rounds of chemotherapy and she said the last two years still feels surreal to her.
“There was a lot of questions,” she said. “A lot of hurt, a lot of anger, a lot of why me? Like, how? I was healthy. I was on a fitness journey.”
![Lydia Whelan](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/08/21/b9891b21-2d0c-3504-a3b2-64c0b4616c56/2aa01d43-88b2-429f-8144-6df50e70343c.jpg)
She added: “It’s been the roughest rollercoaster I could have ever imagined. It’s not something you know how to deal with or are told how to deal with.”
Lydia started her chemotherapy at the end of August 2024 and she gave a devastating insight into how difficult it was.
“It absolutely wipes you, takes away what you see in the mirror,” she said. “I really struggled with that aspect. Still to this day I do. But my friends and my family, the support network I have is amazing.”
Lydia, who also had radiation and surgery, was extremely ill during and towards the end of her chemotherapy and at one point she felt unable to complete another two rounds to take the total to six.
However, while some days she would cry for hours, there were others when she remained positive and looked towards the future. She is now living a beautiful life having completed her treatment.
![Lydia Whelan](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/08/21/b9891b21-2d0c-3504-a3b2-64c0b4616c56/b2723bfe-bcb5-4995-b875-28c75583e904.jpg)
Her house sale went through after Colm had to draw down the mortgage by himself and this December will mark two years since she and Colm moved in together. Lydia must now wait another four years before she can be named on the mortgage when she will officially be in remission.
She now shares her story to raise awareness about breast cancer and in a message to others, she said: “I continue to drive home about checking yourself every month.
“People have come up to me and said, ‘I’m afraid to check myself because of what I’d find.’
“And it’s wild how that’s someone’s thoughts on it. And I’m like, ‘Yeah, but if I didn’t find it when I found it, I would not be here today. There’s no might. I wouldn’t.’
“My cancer was spreading very very fast. I would not be sitting here today.”
She said she now lives her best life, just as she did before her cancer diagnosis, and says “yes to everything”.
Lydia, now 34, added: “It’s given me a new lease of life. As hard as the journey has been, I now don’t stress about the small things. I take a beat. I would have been a very quite anxious and nervous person.”
She added: “I’m still here, I’m still alive, I’m still breathing. I’m just grateful for every day that now if I do have a bad day, I’m angry at myself for having a bad day.
“But as humans, we’re always hard on ourselves. But no, continue to looking forward to even the small things in life.
“A cup of coffee, fresh air, the sun. Little things that we so easily take for granted."
summary: At age 32, Lydia Whelan was diagnosed with aggressive stage two breast cancer just as she and her partner Colm agreed to buy a house. Overwhelmed by the diagnosis and the fear of losing their new home due to mortgage protection issues, she heartbreakingly told her partner to leave her. Following rigorous chemotherapy, radiation, and surgery with the support of her loved ones, Lydia is now a survivor and shares her story to urge others to regularly check themselves for breast cancer.
key_points: Lydia Whelan was diagnosed with aggressive stage two breast cancer at age 32, just a week after she and her partner Colm agreed to buy a house.
Due to mortgage protection complications, Whelan feared losing the home and initially told her partner to leave her.
She underwent intense treatment, including chemotherapy, radiation, and surgery, supported by her family and partner.
Whelan successfully completed her treatment, and Colm secured the mortgage independently so they could move into their home.
She now shares her story to encourage others to regularly check themselves for breast cancer and appreciates life's smaller moments.

title: The unexpected and visible places STIs will show up on your body
author: Alice Giddings
content:
![the concept of prostate and bladder problem, crotch pain of a young person .](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_309142473-4a8c.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
When it comes to sexually transmitted diseases, it’s typically an itching or a burning sensation in your privates that makes you think something’s up.
But, it’s not just our genitals we should be worried about. It turns out there are far more unexpected places on our bodies that symptoms can manifest.
And with 402,000 new STI diagnoses in 2025 alone, it seems some of us may need a refresher course in some of the less obvious signs we might need to go to a sexual health clinic.
‘STIs don’t always follow the textbook pattern people expect,’ superintendent pharmacist at Chemist Click, Abbas Kanani, says.
‘It can affect different parts of the body depending on the type of infection and how it has been transmitted, and it shouldn’t automatically be ruled out as having nothing to do with your sexual health.’
The palms of your hands
A rash on the palms of your hands can actually be a later symptom of syphilis, and it can sometimes spread all over your body. This can develop if the STI has been left untreated.
‘Syphilis is one of those infections that can present in ways people simply would not associate with an STI,’ pharmacist Thorrun Govind tells Metro.
‘Later symptoms can include a rash on the palms of the hands which isn’t usually itchy, but it can be mistaken for a number of more familiar skin conditions like eczema, psoriasis or an allergic reaction.’
![Doctor checking sexually transmitted disease , STD on infected patient skin under magnifying glass](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_309142498-dea7.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
What’s challenging is this rash can look quite different from person to person. While Thorrun explains you cannot catch syphilis from hand-to-hand touching, you could catch it from touching an infected fluid-filled sore called a chancre.
The soles of your feet
Ask Metro
Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.
The soles can also be affected by the characteristic rash seen during secondary syphilis. Again, the rash may spread across the body and can be subtle enough to go unnoticed.
‘A rash on the feet is easy to put down to something like athlete’s foot or irritation from footwear,’ Abbas explains. ‘But if you notice an unusual rash on both the palms and soles, particularly alongside other unexplained symptoms, it’s worth getting it checked rather than assuming it’s simply a skin problem.’
If you have a rash like this which also coincides with swollen glands, tiredness and unprotected sex, you’ll want to get yourself down to clinic for an STI test.
The eyes
Not even our eyeballs are safe when it comes to symptoms from sexually transmitted diseases.
And, this time it’s gonorrhoea that’s the likely culprit. ‘Gonorrhoea can reach the eye if infectious genital fluid is transferred there by the hands,’ Thorrun explains.
![Close up of a woman showing a red infected eye with conjunctivitis. Health care concept](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_309142452-6a76.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
This can cause redness, pain and discharge, and Thorrun adds it can lead to a serious condition called gonococcal conjunctivitis, which requires urgent medical attention to prevent permanent eye damage.
Untreated syphilis can also affect the eyes and cause symptoms such as eye pain, redness and changes in vision.
The throat
Yes, we just gulped, too. But it’s not difficult to realise why a bad throat could be a symptom of an STI.
‘The throat can be exposed to sexually transmitted diseases through oral sex,’ Thorrun explains. ‘Infections such as gonorrhoea, chlamydia, syphilis, herpes and HPV can all affect the throat.’
Superintendent pharmacist Abbas admits that a sore throat is much more likely to be caused by a common respiratory infection than an STI, but says sexual contact can expose the throat to certain infections.’
The joints
This one is much easier to misdiagnose, because some STIs can spread to the joints.
In rare instances, gonorrhoea can spread to the bloodstream and joints, and other STIs can prompt a case of reactive arthritis.
Symptoms can include painful, stiff or swollen joints. ‘Unexplained joint pain isn’t something most people would immediately associate with an STI,’ says Abbas.
‘But, if joint symptoms develop alongside a rash, eye problems, urinary symptoms or other signs of infection, it’s worth seeking medical advice.’
![Close-up of a woman applying topical cream to a cold sore on her lower lip, illustrating personal care, home treatment, skincare routine, minor injury care and medical self-treatment concepts.](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_309142458-c95d.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
The mouth and lips
‘A painless mouth ulcer or sore is very common and usually has nothing to do with an STI,’ Abbas explains. But, the mouth and lips are a very vulnerable spot for sexually transmitted diseases from oral sex.
‘The risk can be higher if there are cuts, sores or broken skin in or around the mouth, because this can provide an easier route for infection,’ Thorrun adds.
For example, syphilis can cause painless sores in areas including the mouth and lips, meaning an infection can sometimes be present without obvious genital symptoms.
‘A persistent or unusual sore, particularly after sexual contact with a new partner, shouldn’t simply be ignored,’ Abbas says. ‘Syphilis sores can be painless, which means people may not recognise them as a sign of infection.’
The anus and rectum
This might be far less surprising, but it’s worth an honourable mention. It’s not just the penis and the vagina that can be affected downstairs, but the anus and rectum, too.
- 
	![Young woman in bed with her arms by her head](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_307896638-cbfc.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0px%2C0px%2C2500px%2C1406px&resize=646%2C363)
- Dirty hotel sex made up for this big disappointment after 10 years of marriage

Gonorrhoea and chlamydia can infect the rectum and can cause symptoms like discharge, soreness, itching, bleeding or pain when passing poo – although many infections also cause no symptoms.
‘People can feel embarrassed talking about symptoms affecting the anus, but they’re important symptoms to mention,’ Abbas says.

- ![Parents can save up to 30% on Kickers school shoes ahead of the new term](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_307346057-1e66.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=960&h=635&crop=1) Parents can save up to 30% on Kickers school shoes ahead of the new term

‘Some infections in this area cause no noticeable symptoms at all, so testing is particularly important following unprotected anal sex or if you’ve been told a partner has an STI.’

summary: Sexually transmitted infections can manifest in various unexpected parts of the body beyond the genitals. According to health experts, symptoms such as rashes, sores, and inflammation can appear on the hands, feet, eyes, throat, joints, and mouth. Recognizing these less obvious signs is crucial for proper testing and treatment.
key_points: Untreated syphilis can cause a non-itchy rash on the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet.
Gonorrhoea can reach the eyes via the hands, potentially causing gonococcal conjunctivitis.
Oral sex can expose the throat and mouth to infections like gonorrhoea, chlamydia, and syphilis, leading to sore throats or painless sores.
Certain STIs can spread to the bloodstream and joints, resulting in painful, stiff, or swollen joints.

title: 'My OCD is so bad I spend seven hours taking a shower'
author: Ciara Healy
content:
'My OCD is so bad I spend seven hours taking a shower' says South Yorkshire woman
South Yorkshire woman describes debilitating OCD
A woman's OCD is so bad she spends seven hours taking a shower.
It has also caused her to have intrusive thoughts about attacking her family members with a kitchen knife.
Victoria Korlewala, aged 20, first began to have symptoms of obsessive-compulsive disorder, a mental health condition characterised by intrusive thoughts and compulsions at age 13, when she became obsessed by the idea that she smelled bad.
![Victoria Korlewala, 20](https://www.thestar.co.uk/jpim-static/image/2026/08/22/9/27/i-have-to-hide-1591181.jpg?trim=0,0,0,0&width=640&quality=65)
![placeholder image](https://www.thestar.co.uk/img/placeholder.jpg)
She then became convinced that she was a "bad person", and was unable to look at a kitchen knife without a graphic image of her using it to stab someone forming in her head.
Victoria, from Doncaster, says her OCD is now so debilitating that it takes her up to seven hours to have a shower, as she is convinced her body is contaminated or dirty.
She is only able to go to the toilet once every two days, as her handwashing routine takes so long, and is hoping to have a catheter fitted to alleviate the pain of having to hold in her wee for so long.
For the last two years she has only left the house for hospital appointments.
Victoria, who is hoping to go to university to study biomedical sciences when her symptoms improve, said: "Every time I'd go into the kitchen, I'd see an image of myself attacking my family with a kitchen knife.
"I had to completely avoid looking at the knives.
"I knew I would never do something like that, but the OCD made it seem so real, and as though it was about to happen.
"My showers take up to seven hours, and I can't go to the bathroom regularly as my handwashing routine takes up to 11 hours."
!["My showers take up to seven hours, and I can't go to the bathroom regularly as my handwashing routine takes up to 11 hours."](https://www.thestar.co.uk/jpim-static/image/2026/08/22/9/15/i-have-to-hide-1589316.jpg?trim=0,0,0,0&width=640&quality=65)
![placeholder image](https://www.thestar.co.uk/img/placeholder.jpg)
When the COVID pandemic hit in 2020, Victoria's symptoms began to ease, as she was no longer around people in school, so she wasn't worried that her classmates were talking about her.
However, in 2021, she started obsessively washing her hands, to the point where she would be late for school due to her handwashing routine.
Around this time, Victoria also began to experience morality OCD, where a person becomes convinced they are a bad person.
She then began to experience harm OCD, a subtype where sufferers experience intrusive thoughts about causing harm to themselves or others.
Every time Victoria would walk into the kitchen and see a kitchen knife, her brain would show her a violent image of herself attacking someone with it.
She went to the doctors, and was diagnosed with OCD in July 2021.
"When I was diagnosed, I felt happy that I wasn't going crazy," she said.
Victoria is currently on anti-depressants and anti-psychotics to try and help manage her condition.
In six month's time, Victoria is set to start inpatient Exposure and Response Prevention therapy (ERP), which helps sufferers to face anxiety-inducing situations whilst resisting compulsions, at Springfield Hospital in Tooting, London, which she hopes will alleviate her symptoms.
Victoria shares insights into how her symptoms affect her daily life on her TikTok channel @victoriaocd to raise awareness that OCD isn’t just about “organising or cleaning”.
summary: Victoria Korlewala, a 20-year-old from Doncaster, suffers from severe obsessive-compulsive disorder that causes debilitating symptoms, including showers lasting up to seven hours and distressing intrusive thoughts of harming her family. Diagnosed with OCD in July 2021, she experiences severe contamination fears, handwashing routines, and morality OCD. She is currently managing her condition with medication and anticipates starting inpatient Exposure and Response Prevention therapy at Springfield Hospital.
key_points: Victoria's OCD symptoms cause her to spend up to seven hours taking a shower due to contamination fears.
She experiences harm OCD, involving intrusive thoughts about attacking her family members with kitchen knives.
Her handwashing routine can take up to 11 hours, limiting her ability to use the bathroom regularly.
She was officially diagnosed with OCD in July 2021 and uses her TikTok channel @victoriaocd to raise awareness about the condition.

title: Chronic illness left me the skinniest I've ever been – I've never felt worse
author: Hannah Van De Peer
content:
![At my slimmest, I was malnourished, and it took a massive toll on my mental health (Picture: Hannah Van De Peer)](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308729878-a387-e1787055438697.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
Stepping on the scales for the first time in 10 days, I saw the result I’d been fearing: I’d lost 21 pounds in under two weeks.
It was June 2025, and I was preparing to have my gallbladder removed. Despite the fact that I was in so much pain and had virtually no appetite, my hospital had put me on a strict, two-week diet to shrink my liver, to make it easier for the surgeon to access the gallbladder itself.
In the Ozempic era, rapid weight loss is seen as an overwhelmingly positive thing. But throughout that diet, I was terrified of losing it too quickly, and the impact it might have on my physical and mental wellbeing.
Sure enough, I soon started experiencing constant fatigue, brain fog, fragile emotions – my hairline even receded. My body wasn’t getting the nutrients it needed to function at a basic level, and my brain was paying the price.
Switching diets and restricting food, sadly, has become my new normal.
In the last two years, I’ve been managing symptoms of four chronic illnesses; during which time, I’ve struggled to maintain my weight.
At my slimmest, I was malnourished, and it took a massive toll on my mental health. I felt exhausted, quick to anger (or break down in tears) for seemingly no reason, and I was trying to push myself to function normally despite the brain fog.
I enjoy being a midsize, curvy woman – because fundamentally, that’s what healthiness looks like to me. But, two years on, my weight is still in a constant state of fluctuation, and the tiredness I feel is second-to-none.
My health woes began in June 2024. Unbeknown to me, I was living with gallbladder disease which was progressing to a dangerous level.
![Hannah Van De Peer: 'Chronic illness left me unable to eat - skinnier doesn?t always mean healthier'](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308729976-f678-e1787055548648.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
Ask Metro
Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.
I had just one gallstone,but it was the size of a golfball and was preventing my gallbladder from working properly, which gave me frequent, excruciating pain attacks and had a domino effect on my appetite.
At the time, I took measures to eliminate all saturated fat and spicy food from my diet, as well as cutting down on alcohol.
I’ve never had any desire to stigmatise food for myself – but I developed a phobia of eating socially in case I’d suffer an attack while out and about.
Birthday meals and date nights became anxiety-inducing – and I’d often find myself leaving sooner than I wanted to.
My biggest fear was – and still is – pain, vomiting or diarrhoea coming out of nowhere, which happened on several occasions. I worry about everything from not having easy access to bathrooms, to how long I’ve spent in the bathroom itself.
While preparing to go out for my ex-partner’s birthday dinner last year, I started suffering from terrible stomach cramps and diarrhoea – which has become my new normal – and I spent the entire Uber ride to the restaurant shaking with anxiety.
‘What if my body betrays me?’ I thought. The pain wasn’t just something I could ignore, it was agonising. I managed to get through it, praying no-one would notice I barely touched my meal.
And, of course, I lost a lot of weight.
![Hannah Van De Peer: 'Chronic illness left me unable to eat - skinnier doesn?t always mean healthier'](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308729975-cb27-e1787055642714.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
To anyone else, dropping from a size 18 to 12 might seem healthy – I was even praised by a neighbour who said I looked ‘great’ – but I was getting more and more frustrated with how physically weak and tired I was, all the time.
Gallbladder surgery was my light at the end of the tunnel. By the time I had to start my NHS-prescribed pre-op meal plan, I was already limited on food choices because of how much pain and discomfort I was in, and I was looking forward to being able to tuck into a gigantic roast dinner when I was well enough to do so.
Unfortunately, though, my health issues didn’t end there.
Two months post-op, I began experiencing more pain – this time at the very top, midsection of my stomach. Again, these were 10-out-of-10 on the pain scale, and would often result in violent vomiting. Sometimes it would start after a glass of wine; occasionally, it would be triggered by stress or a big, bloaty meal.
![Hannah Van De Peer: 'Chronic illness left me unable to eat - skinnier doesn?t always mean healthier'](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308729978-49f3-e1787055398518.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
While my appetite wasn’t necessarily smaller, I was incredibly selective about which food I ‘allowed’ myself to eat. I subscribed to anti-inflammatory diets and would only stick to what I deemed to be ‘safe’ meals.
My symptoms stumped various GPs for months, and I was referred for a gastroscopy – a small camera fed through the throat, into the stomach.
In January 2026, I was diagnosed with stage three gastro-oesophagus reflux disease (GORD) as well as chronic oesophagitis (inflammation in my food pipe), and placed on a lifelong prescription of omeprazole, which decreases stomach acid production.
Even now, I’m in the middle of more abdominal investigations and a potential fourth diagnosis. Food of any type has been causing sudden, intense lower tummy cramps and diarrhoea on a daily basis for months.
![Hannah Van De Peer: 'Chronic illness left me unable to eat - skinnier doesn?t always mean healthier'](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308729977-78fb-e1787055884167.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
My diet – if you can call it that – has been pared down to fruit, plain carbohydrates and protein. Fibre, while healthy and important for most, is a major trigger for me; and, without a gallbladder, I need to be careful about how frequently I tuck into a sweet treat nowadays.
I rarely eat takeaways and restaurants are mostly off-limits, because I need to be aware of every single ingredient.
As a foodie who used to feel genuinely ecstatic about trying new meals, it all feels like a bit of a cosmic joke. My chronic digestive illnesses are debilitating, and it can be exhausting trying to plan my days around them.
I feel like I’ve lost a little part of myself – the person who used to love a morning coffee and croissant, as well as a weekly takeaway without a care in the world, is long gone.
- 
	![Young woman in bed with her arms by her head](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_307896638-cbfc.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0px%2C0px%2C2500px%2C1406px&resize=646%2C363)
- Dirty hotel sex made up for this big disappointment after 10 years of marriage
- I let my 4-year-old have unlimited screen time - I don't care what the experts say
- Iconic '90s chocolate bar with controversial past makes its return to Asda's shelves
Constantly having to keep an eye on my body, in case it decides to freak out, is really fatiguing – and I wish it wasn’t my life.
My weight is still not stable, having recently lost seven pounds in under a month. My confidence now is tied to how physically strong I feel – all I want is to build muscle, not lose fat.
And so I despair when I hear people lauding skinniness as their ultimate goal. Though I appreciate (and feel endless empathy for) those who find Ozempic helpful for existing health issues, it’s hard to not feel frustrated when others treat it as a silver bullet.

- ![Amazon has slashed the price of Cetaphil's bestselling sensitive skin products](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308284045-e781.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=960&h=720&crop=1) Amazon has slashed the price of Cetaphil's bestselling sensitive skin products
- ![Parents can save up to 30% on Kickers school shoes ahead of the new term](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_307346057-1e66.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=960&h=635&crop=1) Parents can save up to 30% on Kickers school shoes ahead of the new term
- ![The back-to-school hack that's helping parents avoid queues and sold-out sizes](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEC_307273147-b677.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=960&h=720&crop=1) The back-to-school hack that's helping parents avoid queues and sold-out sizes
Skinniness, often, isn’t actually the pinnacle of health. That certainly hasn’t been true for me.

Share your views in the comments below.
summary: Managing multiple chronic digestive illnesses, including gallbladder disease and GORD, has caused the author severe weight loss, malnutrition, and significant mental distress. Despite people praising her rapid weight loss, the author emphasizes that being dangerously thin due to illness is far from healthy. Her condition heavily restricts her diet, social life, and daily routine, leaving her exhausted and constantly managing unpredictable physical symptoms.
key_points: The author suffered severe weight loss and malnutrition due to gallbladder disease and subsequent pre-surgery diets.
She was diagnosed with stage three gastro-oesophagus reflux disease (GORD) and chronic oesophagitis in January 2026.
Chronic illness and food triggers have caused extreme social anxiety regarding eating out and public symptoms.
The author stresses that extreme skinniness resulting from illness is not a sign of health and takes a heavy toll on physical and mental wellbeing.

title: I taught myself to wake up without an alarm in a week. Here's how it fixed my sleep
author: Ally Hirschlag
content:
I taught myself to wake up without an alarm in a week. Here's how it fixed my sleep
![Ally Hirschlag Ally Hirshlag, a woman with red curly hair wearing a black sleep mask, wakes up in bed with her cat beside her. She is pulling off her sleep mask (Credit: Ally Hirschlag)](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/images/ic/480xn/p0p5pz0f.jpg.webp) Ally Hirschlag
Ally Hirschlag discovers that waking up naturally can be surprisingly easy, if you take care of other sleep essentials.
My reliance on alarms has varied a lot through my life. When I was a teenager, I habitually woke up on school days before my alarm went off. I wasn't exactly jumping out of bed, but my internal alarm clock was reliable enough that I never worried about being late. That partly had to do with my always-on routine, which typically ended at 11pm, when I would crash out.
Then, in college, my sleep routine broke down due to a less structured schedule, and I began depending far more on my alarm. When I later entered the workforce, I switched back, reverting to a largely consistent sleep schedule and easily waking up alarm-free once again.
In my mid-30s, though, I found myself relying more and more on my alarm, and now I'm past 40, sleep doesn't come as readily at night, while groggy mornings have me regularly mainlining caffeine.
So when my editor suggested I test out learning to wake up without an alarm, based on tips from sleep researchers, I eagerly accepted. My circadian rhythm needed a tune-up, and I was ready to put the work in to fix it.
Finding my rhythm
After talking with experts, I decided a week of no alarms would be a reasonable time to try to reprogramme my own internal alarm. It involved a little preparation, however.
The researchers I spoke with all suggested taking a few days to find my true sleep rhythm before starting (more later on how to adjust your circadian rhythm if this ends up not fitting your schedule).
I typically sleep for seven to eight hours, but my bedtime can be anywhere between 11pm and 2am. Occasionally, I'll fall asleep watching TV on the sofa, only to wake up at 2:30am, which makes it a real challenge to get back to sleep.
Thankfully, I happened to be going on a cruise and had ample time to observe when I naturally felt sleepy at night and ready to wake up in the morning. It turned out to be about 11:30pm and 8am – an eight-and-a-half-hour sleep period.
Getting adequate sleep is vital for our bodies and minds to function properly, and adults should generally aim for seven to nine hours (anything below six increases the risk of premature death by 20%). But there's no magic number that suits everyone.
"Eight [hours] is the middle, but some people are fine with seven, while some need nine," says Eti Ben Simon, associate director of the Sleep Innovation Labs at the University of Texas at Dallas. There will be some biological variability, based on your circadian rhythm, she says.
So how could I maintain this during a work week, when higher anxiety – and worrying about managing to sleep eight hours a night – often impacts my sleep quality?
![Ally Hirschlag To support my new sleep routine, researchers suggested I use blackout blinds, but also to open them first thing in the morning to let in the morning light (Credit: Ally Hirschlag)](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/images/ic/480xn/p0p5pzz1.jpg.webp) Ally Hirschlag
The experts I spoke to say what's important is not just getting enough sleep, but adhering to a consistent schedule. "You want to make sure that you're going to bed at a pretty regular time, and that it's early enough that you'll be able to get that eight [and a half, in my case] hours that you need," says Helen Burgess, co-director of the sleep and circadian research lab at the University of Michigan in the US. "That regular routine will feed back, and often our bodies will start to relax as we get into that routine."
That advice was very reassuring as I was already anxious about potentially waking up too early (something I tend to do when I've an important event the next day).
Light and winding down
My new routine also needed to incorporate natural light, to help sync my internal clock with my sleep schedule. Ideally, these work in tandem, so you're "tired at night and awake during the day", says Simon. Light plays a major role in this partnership by activating the hormones that signal sleep and wakefulness.
"Light is the single biggest regulator of the circadian clock," says Anna Joyce, a chartered psychologist, sleep specialist and researcher at Regent's University London. "It tells melatonin to turn off, and that it's time to be awake." Studies have also shown that bright morning light can have a significant antidepressant effect by providing a healthy dose of serotonin.
I'm quite light-sensitive, so the researchers I spoke to suggested using blackout blinds (which I already had) while sleeping, and I decided to wear my sleep mask for added protection. Then, upon waking, they recommended I immediately open the blinds to let in the morning light, which triggers a surge of cortisol, a hormone that allows us to be alert and ready for action. "That helps tell the clock, 'Okay, this is when I start my day'," says Simon.
Joyce also stressed the importance of having a "predictable wind-down routine" within approximately two hours of when you want to be asleep. Exactly what works here will vary person by person, but dimming the lights is key, as it signals your body to produce melatonin, prepping you for sleep. I planned to get into PJs, brush my teeth and do my skincare regimen as soon as I felt sleepy, so I could simply climb into bed at my designated bedtime.
Simon advised paying attention to my body's temperature. At night, our core temperature drops because we're exerting less energy, and the body releases lingering energy through the hands and feet via vasodilation (widening of blood vessels). This is why it's harder to fall or stay asleep when it's hot. Overheating absolutely disrupts my sleep, so I set our thermostat to drop earlier than usual, at 11pm, and outfitted our bed with thermoregulating bamboo sheets.
Sleep obstacles
My biggest sleep impediment, though, is my smartphone. That's a common complaint, according to the experts I spoke to.
The blue light devices emit may be partly responsible: it's on a similar wavelength to daylight, which can send confusing signals to the brain when it's nighttime. The likely more impactful aspect of smartphones, though, is dopamine scrolling, aka habitually scanning social media feeds to chase small hits of good feelings. Algorithms on these platforms are designed to keep us engaged, so it's not surprising that a recent analysis found that excessive scrolling inhibits sleep.
![Ally Hirschlag During the experiment I aimed to eat meals at a consistent time and finish dinner at least three hours before bed (Credit: Ally Hirschlag)](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/images/ic/480xn/p0p5q011.jpg.webp) Ally Hirschlag
To overcome this obstacle, I used a physical app-blocking device, scheduling my block from 9pm to 12pm every night of the experiment. I also put my phone into greyscale mode (typically found in your accessibility settings, if you're interested) to make the imagery look duller and less attention worthy.
I restricted myself to one cup of coffee a day in the morning, aimed to eat meals at a consistent time and finish dinner at least three hours before bed (since your metabolism influences your circadian rhythm). Burgess also suggested I avoid alcohol as much as possible. "It will actually help you fall asleep a little bit faster," she says, but "messes up your sleep later on", as it suppresses REM sleep.
Before kicking off the experiment, I noted where it could go awry. We have two cats that like breakfast at 6am. Thankfully, they're mostly programmed to wake my husband up for this (I'm the evening feeder). His gentle early-morning alarm rarely wakes me, but he offered to sleep on the couch whenever he was getting up egregiously early (5am).
And finally, at the recommendation of all the experts I spoke to, I set an emergency alarm 20 minutes later than my desired 8am natural wakeup time, just in case.
A seven-day test
On the first night, I was asleep by midnight, half an hour after my target of 11:30pm, though I woke a few times during the night. That morning, I awoke slightly before 8am but snoozed until 8.15am. I fell asleep around the same time the second night, but it took some coercion – listening to an ASMR (autonomous sensory meridian response) video with my phone turned upside down conked me out. I ended up sleeping until my emergency alarm at 8:20am.
Day three was quite busy, so I fell asleep around 11pm, and woke up naturally at 7:10am. Since I didn't need to be up yet, I lingered a bit in bed, but didn't fall back asleep.
The key thing about sleep is it's not an on and off switch.
Life inevitably threw some hurdles. By night four, I had no trouble falling asleep a bit before midnight. The next morning, however, I was woken up at 6:45am by an offensively early doorbell (I did still manage to fall back asleep for a further hour).
Night five had me asleep by 11:30pm and awake the next morning at 8:12am, despite a brief cat paw to the face at 5:30am. Night six was my birthday, so I had a couple of drinks and was in bed by 12:30am. I woke up with some heartburn at 6am (which I considered karmic punishment for deviating from the experiment), then fell back asleep until 9am.
![Ally Hirschlag I put my phone in greyscale mode in the evening – and locked it in a physical app blocking device from 9pm to stop myself dopamine scrolling (Credit: Ally Hirschlag)](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/images/ic/480xn/p0p5q026.jpg.webp) Ally Hirschlag
On night seven, a Friday, I fell asleep easily between 11:30pm and 12am, and woke up Saturday morning at 8:05am. It's a rare occasion for me to be up before my husband on a weekend, so I went to get us cortados from around the corner.
My week-long experiment had officially wrapped, but I still woke up comfortably a few minutes after 8am on Sunday, and this continued into the following week with little effort. In the weeks following, I've maintained some of the expert-recommended sleep hygiene routines, like regular mealtimes and less phone use before bed. I've somewhat reverted to alarm wakeups but have had much less of a struggle naturally waking up when I want to – as long as I've had at least eight hours of sleep.
My big takeaways
My internal clock was by no means a German train by the end of the experiment, but it still felt successful overall. I had less trouble waking up naturally around 8am and felt less morning grogginess by day four. What helped the most, I felt, was the regular bedtime routine and limiting screen exposure.
I plan to keep this up as much as I can, even on weekends: it legitimately left me feeling more rested and energised. Eventually, I'd like to shift my wake-up time an hour earlier, though Burgess says that can be a slow process. "The circadian system is slow to shift. I would say start with a half-hour shift in both bedtime and wake time, half an hour earlier each day until you get to where you want to be, and then try to hold it," she suggests.
More like this:
With all that life throws at us, from doorbells to birthdays to stress, consistent, truly restful sleep can be an elusive commodity. While exploring the scientific research for this article, what struck me most was how strained our relationship is with sleep today.
Over-reliance on tech is impacting sleep quality, especially in adolescents, whose developing brains and bodies need sleep more than any other demographic. A 2025 analysis of a survey of 45,000 Norwegian students found that excessive smartphone use was directly correlated with poor sleep.
"We do see a strong link between these mental health disorders and sleep disruptions in young adults, and we also see that if you have any tendency or any risk for mental health disorders, sleep loss can push you over the edge," says Simon. "They need at least nine hours of sleep, about 70% don't even get to seven."
Many adolescents could certainly benefit from a sleep recalibration week. It was worth it for me, though I recognise that finding the time is a luxury not everyone can afford.
Still, incorporating any of these habits into your daily routine could help in finding a more restful night, and an easier wake-up.
If your sleep schedule is off, and you do have some room to try a reset, be patient with yourself. It might take some trial and error to discover your own unique rhythm. "The key thing about sleep is it's not an on and off switch," says Burgess. "It doesn't quite work that way."
--
For trusted insights on health and wellbeing, sign up to the Health Fix newsletter by senior health correspondent Melissa Hogenboom who also writes the Live Well For Longer and Six Steps to Calm courses.
summary: An author undertook a week-long experiment to reprogram her circadian rhythm and wake up naturally without an alarm clock, guided by sleep researchers. By establishing a consistent bedtime routine, incorporating natural light exposure, managing room temperature, and limiting evening smartphone use, she successfully reduced morning grogginess and improved her ability to wake up naturally. Following the experiment, she maintained several of these improved sleep hygiene habits to feel more rested and energized.
key_points: Light serves as the primary regulator of the circadian clock, with morning light signaling the body to suppress melatonin and increase alertness.
A consistent bedtime schedule helps the body relax and naturally aligns the internal clock for adequate rest.
Evening smartphone use, including blue light exposure and dopamine scrolling, negatively impacts sleep quality.
Additional sleep hygiene measures such as finishing dinner three hours before bed, keeping the bedroom cool, and setting an emergency backup alarm supported the experiment's success.

title: The three ‘primary drivers’ behind cancer cases in men, according to scientists
author: Storm Newton
content:
Men with heart disease are at a higher risk of developing and dying from cancer, new research suggests.
Researchers identified smoking, obesity and drinking too much alcohol as “primary drivers” behind cases in men, with the link most pronounced in lung and oesophageal cancers.
Experts called for "more to be done" to manage these risks, such as targeted screening interventions.
The study, conducted by researchers at the University of Aberdeen and Keele University, examined how cancer risk and mortality differed between men and women over more than 25 years.
It drew on data from 22,534 people taking part in the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer (EPIC)-Norfolk study.
Almost 11,000 either had cardiovascular disease (CVD), an umbrella term for conditions affecting the heart or blood vessels, at the start of the study, or developed it during monitoring.
The study found the lifetime risk of developing cancer among those with CVD was higher in men (17.3 per cent) compared with women (12.8 per cent).
In those without CVD, the risk of cancer was 10.2 per cent for men and 8.2 per cent for women.
![More than eight million people - four million men and four million women - are living with CVD in the UK](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/05/19/16/55/PA-84260452.jpeg)
Dr Tiberiu Pana, specialty registrar in cardiology at NHS Grampian, and honorary early career clinical research fellow at the University of Aberdeen, said: “We found that cancer incidence and death were higher in people with cardiovascular disease than in those without – a relationship we already knew a bit about.
“However, through looking at this large patient group over a very long period of time, we were able to examine it more thoroughly.
“We have identified clear differences between men and women across a range of factors in those with cardiovascular disease and all types of cancer.”
Further analysis of cancers found outside of the reproductive system found that people with heart disease faced higher rates of gastric, oesophageal, lung, bowel and non-melanoma skin cancers. These were also more prominent among men, according to the study.
Men with CVD also had an increased risk of dying from gastric, oesophageal, and lung cancers compared with those without heart disease.
Researchers said this “may be partly driven by common risk factors” between CVD and cancer.
The findings, published in the European Heart Journal, suggest the “primary drivers” of cancer cases and cancer deaths in men with heart disease were smoking, obesity and drinking too much alcohol, they added.
Who is at risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD)?
NHS
There are things that may make it more likely you'll get CVD, including:
- your lifestyle – such as smoking, drinking too much alcohol, being overweight and not being active
- your age – CVD mainly affects people over 50 years old
- your sex – men are more likely to get CVD than women
- your ethnicity – you may be more likely to get CVD if you're from a South Asian, Black African or African Caribbean ethnic background
- having family members with CVD
- having certain conditions, such as diabetes, high blood pressure or high cholesterol
Dr Rosa Thuemmler, of the University of Aberdeen, said: “We found that men had a higher incidence of both getting cancer in the first place and sadly, also in dying from it, and this was particularly true among people with cardiovascular disease.
“Although the pattern was the same across all subtypes of cancer, this was most pronounced in lung and oesophageal cancers.”
According to the British Heart Foundation, more than eight million people – four million men and four million women – are living with CVD in the UK.
Professor Phyo Myint, of the University of Aberdeen, said: “More needs to be done to improve risk management, targeted screening and prevention to address this health inequality.”
Mamas Mamas, professor of cardiology at Keele University, said: “We need to better understand the driver of cancer development in these populations.
“Furthermore, whilst cardio-oncology services have focused mainly on cancer patients preventing the development of cardiovascular diseases, we need better pathways that can identify and prevent cancer development in patients with cardiac conditions.”
Nicola Smith, senior health information manager at Cancer Research UK, said: “Many causes of cancer and heart disease overlap, which may explain why there’s a link between the two, and both of these diseases are more common in people from deprived areas.
“Cancer is slightly more likely to affect men, partly because smoking rates are higher, but more research is needed before we can say that there is a stronger link between cancer and heart disease in men compared to women.
“If anyone is concerned about their risk of cancer or heart disease, there are proven steps they can take to reduce it.
“These include not smoking, keeping a healthy weight, and cutting down on alcohol.”
summary: New research from the University of Aberdeen and Keele University shows that men with heart disease face a higher risk of developing and dying from cancer than women. Researchers identified smoking, obesity, and excessive alcohol consumption as primary drivers behind these cancer cases, with the strongest links seen in lung and oesophageal cancers. Experts are calling for improved risk management, targeted screening, and better healthcare pathways to address these overlapping conditions.
key_points: Men with cardiovascular disease have a higher lifetime risk of developing cancer compared to women.
Smoking, obesity, and excessive alcohol intake were identified as primary drivers for cancer cases in men with heart disease.
The link between heart disease and cancer was most pronounced in lung and oesophageal cancers.
Researchers and health experts are calling for improved risk management, prevention, and targeted screening interventions.

title: What Happens to Your Blood Pressure When You Eat Bananas Every Day
author: Melissa Mitri; M S; RD
content:
Getty Images. EatingWell Design.
- Bananas are rich in potassium, which helps balance sodium for healthy blood pressure.
- They have antioxidants and fiber that support heart health and a healthy gut microbiome.
- People with kidney issues or on certain meds should consult a doctor before eating bananas.
When it comes to lowering blood pressure, we hear a lot about the importance of reducing sodium intake. However, we don’t hear nearly as much about another blood pressure–lowering measure: Increasing potassium. Yet research reveals that adding more potassium to your plate can be an easy (and tasty!) way to keep your blood pressure numbers in check.
Nearly half of adults in the U.S. are living with high blood pressure (aka hypertension).potassium-rich fruits around. Yet, many of us avoid these healthy fruits. Dietitians, like Michelle Routhenstein, M.S., RD, CDCES, say it’s time to bring them back to the table. “Bananas often get a bad rap for their sugar content, but they are known to help lower blood pressure in several ways,” she says.
Keep reading to learn what makes them so great for blood pressure, plus even more blood pressure–friendly fruits to add to your day.
3 Ways Bananas May Impact Blood Pressure
They May Help You Excrete Sodium
Studies show that most Americans consume too much sodium, which is linked to higher blood pressure.offset the negative effects of sodium. How so? “Bananas are rich in potassium, a mineral that helps lower blood pressure by filtering sodium out of the kidneys, restoring fluid balance and relaxing blood vessels,” says Sheri Gaw, RDN, CDCES.
One medium banana contains about 420 milligrams of potassium. So, slice one into your cereal or over a bowl of yogurt. Add sliced bananas to a peanut butter or almond butter sandwich. Or, toss banana chunks into your favorite smoothie. They’re a super-satisfying way to support healthy blood pressure.
They Can Relax Your Blood Vessels
Potassium in bananas helps balance sodium levels in the body, which, in turn, helps relax blood vessel walls.
But it’s not just the potassium in bananas that’s responsible for these benefits. Bananas are also a surprising source of antioxidants, especially catechins, which help your blood vessels dilate.reduce oxidative stress and inflammation in the blood vessel walls, both of which can contribute to high blood pressure, says Routhenstein.
They Help Promote Gut Health
“Emerging research suggests a healthy gut may be linked to lower blood pressure,” says Routhenstein. Turns out, bananas can help with that, too. One medium banana contains 3 grams of gut-friendly fiber. And if you’re OK eating your bananas before they’re fully ripe, they also provide resistant starch, a unique type of fiber that helps feed your good gut bacteria, helping them grow and thrive.
Related Stories
![A man holding a mug and eating from a bowl with a spoon](<https://www.eatingwell.com/thmb/g_AKOZ4uAP5FcogcOOvGqJZYuuk=/300x200/filters:no_upscale():max_bytes(150000):strip_icc()/Foods-Men-Should-Eat-Every-Week-for-Better-Blood-Pressure-163333cc1fd64eeba2de05505c5c2b83.jpg>) 
![Person holding a cup of hibiscus tea at a table indoors](<https://www.eatingwell.com/thmb/c9YlQAdPMe31hXsTlqPcgAAeqUc=/300x200/filters:no_upscale():max_bytes(150000):strip_icc()/What-Happens-to-Your-Blood-Pressure-When-You-Drink-Hibiscus-Tea-According-to-Dietitians-7146c1406c874d11a0b96fd67e87efb2.jpg>) 
Is It Safe to Eat Bananas Everyday?
Gaw says that for most people, eating a daily banana is generally safe and can be a great way to boost fiber, vitamins, minerals and antioxidants.
Routhenstein agrees and notes eating a banana a day is OK for most healthy adults, and can be beneficial due to its potassium and antioxidant content. However, both experts say that eating lots of bananas may not be ideal for certain people, such as those with diabetes, kidney disorders or who take certain medications.
For example, for those with diabetes, a banana may cause blood sugar to spike, says Gaw. This is especially likely if it’s not paired with a source of protein and fat, such as a tablespoon of peanut butter, a handful of nuts or a slice of cheese, she explains. She adds that those with kidney disorders may need to limit bananas, as kidney disease makes it harder for the kidneys to clear potassium from the body, which can lead to heart and muscle issues.
Routhenstein stresses that people taking medication that may increase blood potassium levels, or who need to restrict their potassium intake, should consult their health care provider to see if bananas are safe for them to eat.
Medications that may raise blood potassium include:
- Angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, such as benazepril (Lotensin)
- Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), like losartan (Cozaar)
- Potassium-sparing diuretics, such as amiloride (Midamor) and spironolactone (Aldactone)
- Loop and thiazalide diuretics, like furosemide (Lasix), bumetanide (Bumex), chlorothiazide (Diuril) and metolazone (Zaroxolyn)
Other Blood Pressure–Friendly Fruits to Consider
Bananas are a great choice for healthy blood pressure, but they’re not the only fruits that can help keep your numbers in check. For additional blood pressure–lowering power, try these fruits.
- Pomegranates. Pomegranates are rich in antioxidants called polyphenols, which may help lower blood pressure. While most of the research on pomegranates and blood pressure has been conducted using pomegranate juice, adding some juicy (and fiber-rich!) pomegranate seeds to your day certainly couldn’t hurt.
- Kiwis. Gaw notes kiwis are high in vitamin C and contain compounds like actinidin, which support nitric oxide production. That’s key, as nitric oxide helps blood vessels dilate more effectively to reduce pressure on vessel walls.
- Oranges. These juicy citrus fruits are loaded with vitamin C (nearly an entire day’s worth in one fruit!). They also give you a decent chunk of potassium and fiber. Because they’re sturdy, they don’t bruise easily. So, they’re easy to toss into your backpack or bag for healthy snacking on the go.
- Berries. “Berries are rich in plant compounds, vitamins and minerals which help blood vessels to relax and lower blood pressure,” says Gaw. While all berries are good, wild blueberries may be especially beneficial. One study found that older adults who consumed a daily wild blueberry powder supplement for 12 weeks (equivalent to slightly more than 1 cup of wild blueberries) experienced reductions in systolic blood pressure.
Recipes to Try
![Recipe image of No-Sugar-Added High-Protein Strawberry Shake.](<https://www.eatingwell.com/thmb/dwZdyLl8XT05nsUT287QZ7x3xZ8=/300x200/filters:no_upscale():max_bytes(150000):strip_icc()/No-Sugar-Added-High-Protein-StrawberryShake-beauty-37456_preview_maxWidth_4000_maxHeight_4000_ppi_300_quality_100-4e1ba78266934792b1894e8125c1d17a.jpg>) 
![Berry-Almond Smoothie Bowl](<https://www.eatingwell.com/thmb/s0crQRNsbufnDwRYNgXZju-M5oM=/300x200/filters:no_upscale():max_bytes(150000):strip_icc()/7881886-c9dffe4276184c12b0bd1812afdbd9f2.jpg>) 
![an image of the Banana Overnight Oats](<https://www.eatingwell.com/thmb/G_YOuz-X0BcRCp-o96-4VSiJBoE=/300x200/filters:no_upscale():max_bytes(150000):strip_icc()/EWL-banana-overnight-oats-beauty-148_preview_maxWidth_4000_maxHeight_4000_ppi_300_quality_100-2231fcbf1ed74681a1902a4ebf5bfdf6.jpg>) 
Our Expert Take
A daily banana can be a delicious, satisfying way to support your blood pressure. Bananas are rich in blood pressure–friendly potassium and contain compounds that relax your blood vessels. That’s not all. Their unique fibers may also promote healthy blood pressure by favorably influencing the gut microbiome. If lower blood pressure is a goal, don’t stop with bananas. Pomegranates, kiwis, oranges and berries are also filled with nutrients that can do your blood pressure good. While most healthy people can safely enjoy a banana—or other potassium-rich fruits—every day, speak with your health care provider if you have diabetes, kidney disease or take certain medications, such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs or diuretics, to find out what’s best for your unique health needs.
summary: Eating a daily banana can help support healthy blood pressure because the fruit is rich in potassium, antioxidants, and fiber. Potassium helps the body excrete excess sodium and relaxes blood vessel walls, while fiber promotes a healthy gut microbiome linked to lower blood pressure. However, individuals with diabetes, kidney disorders, or those taking specific medications should consult a doctor before making bananas a daily habit.
key_points: Bananas are rich in potassium, which helps filter sodium out of the kidneys and restore fluid balance.
Antioxidants in bananas, such as catechins, help reduce oxidative stress and dilate blood vessels.
Bananas contain fiber and resistant starch that support a healthy gut microbiome, which is linked to lower blood pressure.
People with kidney issues, diabetes, or those taking certain medications like ACE inhibitors should consult a doctor before eating bananas daily.

title: I went for an eye test and discovered I had a brain tumour the size of a lemon
author: Alison Bartlett
content:
![Alison Bartlett](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/health-fitness/2026/08/17/TELEMMGLPICT000497959848_17869749891160_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqKrVQ3kpMSBXudFn-LKazWaBaCuyZikPrjFVhkKG8zak.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Alison Bartlett](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/health-fitness/2026/08/17/TELEMMGLPICT000497959848_17869749891160_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqKrVQ3kpMSBXudFn-LKazWaBaCuyZikPrjFVhkKG8zak.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
When I started suffering from intense migraines, I put them down to stress. After all, we were in the midst of the Covid pandemic and my (now) husband, Richard, and I had just discovered that our house purchase had fallen through. We were stuck in limbo, living with his parents while trying to continue to work from home and find somewhere new to live.
But over the following months the migraines became more frequent and I developed a string of strange symptoms, including dizzy head rushes, cloudy vision and unexplained weight gain. Eventually, I booked an appointment with my local optician. I never imagined that less than 24 hours later I’d be in hospital, after an eye scan revealed signs of a brain tumour the size of a lemon.
My migraines wouldn’t go away
Before Covid, Richard and I lived together in London. He worked as a research director for a consultancy firm and I was a graphic designer specialising in print and digital marketing. Our house purchase fell through when the pandemic hit. Fortunately, we were able to move in with Richard’s parents and could continue working remotely, while settling into a new routine.
Then, in June, the migraines started. My dad has suffered from migraines for years and I’d experienced the occasional one myself, but these were unlike anything I’d had before. Every couple of weeks I’d be left unable to work or even hold a conversation. I’d shut myself away in the makeshift bedroom Richard and I shared, lying in the dark with my eyes closed until the pain eased.
Around the same time, I also started gaining weight. Richard’s mother cooked comforting home-cooked meals, often followed by pudding, and with us exercising far less than usual that seemed easy to explain. By the time we eventually moved into our new home, in October, I’d gained around 3st 2lb.
I was emotionally absent
Once we’d settled into our new two-bedroom detached house in Bicester, I expected everything to improve. Instead, the migraines continued. Richard encouraged me to see our GP, but I was reluctant. At the time, the NHS was still under enormous pressure following the pandemic and I convinced myself it wasn’t serious enough to warrant an appointment.
![Alison Bartlett and](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/health-fitness/2026/08/17/TELEMMGLPICT000497959831_17869814938190_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwSX5rhseiWKOo9p9OQ-ymek.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Eventually, however, I went. After a quick consultation, I was diagnosed with migraines, prescribed medication and reassured that the tablets should help. In hindsight, I wish I had pushed for a more thorough examination, but I accepted the prescription and hoped things would improve. Unfortunately, they didn’t.
At the start of 2021, I developed what I called “wobbly leg syndrome”, where my knee would suddenly give way when I stood up. Most mornings I woke with dark patches clouding my vision, and I regularly experienced dizzy head rushes.
The biggest change in me, though, wasn’t physical. Looking back, I now know the tumour was affecting my frontal lobe and changing my personality. I became increasingly withdrawn and apathetic. I stopped caring that I felt ill and had little energy or motivation to cook, exercise or even help around the house.
Richard did everything he could to support me, gently encouraging me to go back to the doctor, but I simply couldn’t bring myself to do it. At the time, I thought I was depressed. It wasn’t until much later that I understood the tumour itself was responsible for so much of how I’d been feeling.
The months after moving into our first home together should have been exciting. We should have been wandering around town choosing furniture and paint colours. Instead, I spent most of that time emotionally absent, while Richard desperately tried to help me find my way back.
The eye test that changed everything
For more than a year, I refused to seek any further medical advice. By August 2022, Richard had reached breaking point. He called my dad, who lives in South Africa, and explained everything that had been happening. My dad immediately contacted a doctor friend, who gave one piece of advice: I needed to see a professional as soon as possible.
Hearing how worried they both were finally persuaded me. A few weeks later, I spoke to a private doctor who referred me to a neurologist. He recommended I have an OCT scan at my local optician before arranging an MRI. The scan creates detailed images of the retina and optic nerve, helping detect problems such as swelling behind the eye.
So, I booked an appointment at my local Specsavers in Bicester. The scan itself took only a couple of minutes. Afterwards, though, the optician called the manager in to see me. “You need to go to John Radcliffe Hospital today or tomorrow at the latest,” she told me. “Both of your optic nerves are swollen.”
Most people would have panicked. Strangely, I barely reacted. By then I was so detached from everything around me that I simply couldn’t process how serious the situation was. The next day, I went to hospital where further tests were carried out before I was referred to St Mary’s Hospital in Paddington for an MRI scan.
![Alison Bartlett eye scan](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/07/28/TELEMMGLPICT000496741342_17852494861446_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq7t4Eljyiy6iRMFuEKY2dXA1vLvhkMtVb21dMmpQBfEs.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
A frightening diagnosis
The scan took place the following Sunday. Afterwards, Richard and I sensed something wasn’t right. Although the radiographers couldn’t discuss the images, we were told that “something was there” and they arranged an urgent neurology appointment for two days later. I was also prescribed steroids to reduce the swelling while doctors investigated further.
Even then, I struggled to grasp the seriousness of what I was being told. At the appointment, the neurologist confirmed I had a benign brain tumour measuring 6cm across – roughly the size of a lemon. The tumour was pressing against my pituitary gland and affecting my frontal lobe, explaining the migraines, vision problems, weight gain and dramatic changes in my mood and personality.
As frightening as the diagnosis was, it also brought enormous relief. After more than two years, at the age of 42, everything finally made sense. Two days later, I met my neurosurgeon to discuss the operation. Fortunately, years of watching Grey’s Anatomy meant I wasn’t especially squeamish. I was fascinated to learn how the surgeons would carefully access my brain, remove as much of the tumour as possible and reconstruct everything afterwards.
The operation
On the following Tuesday, Richard dropped me off at Charing Cross Hospital ahead of surgery. The next morning, I remember being wheeled into theatre, meeting my neurosurgeon and then drifting off under general anaesthetic.
After 11 hours in theatre, I woke up feeling surprisingly comfortable. Along my scalp I could feel there were around 60 staples holding everything together, but the pain was nowhere near as bad as I’d imagined.
![Alison Bartlett](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/07/28/TELEMMGLPICT000496741350_17852494857800_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqv3bZLUcinocdxThoasxukcwZgCewa-xkrckcIXHk6m8.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
During the operation, doctors had also performed a lumbar puncture to measure and relieve the pressure of the fluid surrounding my brain. Ironically, that proved more painful than the surgery.
Richard visited as soon as he could and, over the next nine days in hospital, I began feeling better than I had in years. The migraines disappeared. My vision cleared. It genuinely felt as though someone had lifted a weight off my shoulders.
When I was discharged, I walked slowly because my back was still sore from the lumbar puncture, but otherwise I already felt like a different person. Over the following months, I gradually returned to work and regained my strength. As my hormones stabilised and my energy returned, the weight I’d gained naturally disappeared too.
![Alison Bartlett brain scan](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/07/28/TELEMMGLPICT000496741346_17852494859303_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqUdzhVSO1dBnYosldNXMOeZOZvj214O3LJs23BwERrf4.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Within a year, I was back to my previous weight, but more importantly I felt like my happy self again. Friends and family all commented that the old Alison had returned.
Making the most of every day
Richard and I have our lives back now. He proposed in January 2024 and we got married this June. I jokingly told everyone I was waiting until my scalp had healed and my hair had grown back before walking down the aisle – but it did.
